SNOW SQUALL. A brief period of heavy snow occurred across Adams County as a cold front moved across the region. In the snow squalls, snowfall rates were around two inches an hour, the wind gusted to around 40 mph and the visibility was reduced to under a mile. The snow squall was followed by a period of 40 to 50 mph wind gusts into the early evening.

In the snow squalls, snowfall rates were around two inches an hour, the wind gusted to around 40 mph and the visibility was reduced to under a mile. The snow squall was followed by a period of 40 to 50 mph wind gusts into the early evening. The automated weather observing equipment at the Black River Falls airport measured a wind gust of 52 mph.

One person was killed in a two vehicle accident in Winona. The driver lost control on snow and ice covered roads and slammed into the rear of a parked semi. A mixture of freezing rain, sleet and snow occurred from the evening of February 21st into the evening of the 22nd and was responsible for creating the hazard driving conditions.

A total of ten people were injured in a three vehicle accident in Rochester. The first vehicle lost control on a snow covered road, slid into the path of a school bus and then collided with another vehicle. Seven children on the bus were injured in the accident. A light snow event from the afternoon of February 24th into the morning of the 25th caused the roads to be snow covered and slippery.
COOP and volunteer snow observers reported that around 6 inches of snow fell across Clayton County.
COOP and volunteer snow observers reported that 5 to 7 inches of snow fell across Grant County. The highest reported total was 7 inches near Platteville.

Up to 1.5 inches of rain fell across the area in early March. With the ground still frozen, the resulting runoff pushed the Trempealeau River out of its banks in Arcadia. The river crested just over the flood stage at 8.15 feet.

Runoff after a rainfall event pushed the Black River out of its banks in Black River Falls. The river crested over a foot above the flood stage at 48.36 feet on the 24th.
Runoff after a rainfall event pushed the Black River out of its banks near Galesville. The river crested almost a half foot above the flood stage at 12.44 feet on the 26th.
Runoff after a rainfall event pushed the Yellow River out of its banks in Necedah. The river crested a half foot above the flood stage at 15.49 feet on the 27th.

This EF2 tornado formed southwest of Taopi and quickly intensified and caused significant damage in Taopi. Most buildings were damaged and 10 were destroyed. Cars were tossed, grain bins destroyed, and numerous trees and power lines downed. Two people were injured seeking shelter from the storm when they became trapped under debris. Just outside of Taopi, part of the roof was removed from a farmhouse, several outbuildings were damaged, and several head of cattle were missing.
An estimated 60 mph wind gust occurred at the fire station in Charles City.

An EF1 tornado formed southwest of Spring Valley and moved almost due north before dissipating west of Spring Valley. The tornado blew down a barn and damaged several other farm buildings along its path. Several new power poles along County Highway 1 were leaning after the storm.

An EF1 tornado developed just to the southwest of Mauston and tracked northeast before dissipating just west of the Wisconsin River south of Castle Lake Dam. In Mauston, the tornado caused roof damage to the hospital and a restaurant, blew windows out of several vehicles near the hospital, took down several stop lights, blew over parked semis, snapped power poles and downed several trees in a mobile home park that damaged numerous homes. In Veteran's Memorial Park, stands for the baseball field were overturned with some blown across the street and the scoreboard was ripped off its posts. A tree fell on the roof of an apartment complex damaging the roof and allowing water to leak into some units. Northeast of Mauston over rural parts of Juneau County, the damage was mainly limited to trees. The mayor of Mauston issued a disaster declaration.
A funnel cloud was sighted near Adams.

An EF1 tornado developed east of La Farge and moved northeast along State Highway 82 before dissipating north of White City. A house, farm outbuildings and a couple of campers were damaged along with numerous trees.

An EF2 tornado developed south of Tomah and moved northeast before crossing into Juneau County north of Shennington. The tornado crossed Interstates 90 & 94 and passed just to the east of Wyeville. Along its path, extensive tree damage occurred with some downed trees landing on homes, numerous semis were tipped over along  Interstate 90/94 resulting in two injuries, a metal farm shed near Oakdale had several pieces of metal removed, and a few structures near Wyeville sustained damage, including at least one farm outbuilding that was destroyed. Up to three hour delays occurred along Interstate 90 after the tornado moved through. Monroe County declared a state of emergency.

In and near Calmar, several buildings sustained wind damage and numerous trees were blown down. The roof was blown off a house, a business lost part of its roof, a system to move grain between storage silos was destroyed, a metal silo collapsed, the side of another silo was blown in, and a portion of the roof was removed from a large barn. At the community college, numerous buildings sustained roof and siding damage with doors blown in, windows broken, and a couple of vehicles were also blown over. The public schools sustained damage to their athletic fields. Metal bleachers at the softball field were blown over and pushed through a chain link fence. At the football field, the new press box was blown off the top of the stadium and two metal light poles were downed. Some rooftop air conditioning units were flipped over on the high school building.

A tornado touched down in Grant County across the Wisconsin River from Wauzeka, WI (Crawford County). The tornado touch down was brief, as witnessed by a Grant County sheriff, and in a fairly remote area of Wisconsin DNR managed land. The touch down was about 1.8 miles south of Wauzeka in northern Grant County at 1:52 p.m. CDT. The tornado was recorded as an EF0 intensity  (65 to 85 mph winds). This supercell thunderstorm continued to produce funnels on its track east along the Wisconsin River through Boscobel and Muscoda (Grant County). No additional tornadoes were confirmed however.
In addition to the hail, 2.7 inches of rain fell.

A tornado occurred at 5:45 p.m. CDT in La Crosse County, WI, near Barre Mills and it was surveyed by a National Weather Service meteorologist on Sunday, June 8th.  The tornado initially touched down just west of Russian Coulee Road approximately two miles east of Barre Mills (La Crosse County).  There the tornado destroyed one metal barn and partially unroofed another.  Much of the debris from the first barn was thrown to the north; however, some of its debris was scattered to the east for nearly a half mile up a hill.  A family of five heard the tornado and they took cover in a basement.  Fortunately no one was injured.||The tornado then proceeded over a hill and moved through another farmstead.  It destroyed a barn and unroofed much of the adjacent house.  Both soft and hardwood trees were either snapped or uprooted.  ||The tornado then moved through several wooded areas as it crossed County Road II, Antony Road, County Road II again, and then Highway 162 near Souchek Road.||The path of this tornado was about 6 miles long with an average width of 600 feet.  It has an EF1 rating (estimated wind speeds of 90 to 110 mph).  Several nearby neighbors saw the tornado as it moved through both farmsteads.

A brief tornado touched down about 2 to 3 miles northwest of Stacyville, as reported by law enforcement officials and storm spotters. The Stacyville police chief photographed the tornado. There was no damage reported.

Law enforcement officials and the public confirmed a tornado touched down briefly just northwest of Perkins. The tornado was captured on video and lasted only a couple seconds. No damage was reported.

Abnormally dry conditions with rainfall totals 3 to 5 inches below normal for the month of June resulted in severe drought conditions for 88 square miles across eastern Dodge County towards the start of July. The anomalously dry conditions continued through July with rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches below normal. This resulted in all of Dodge County experiencing at least severe drought conditions, with far eastern Dodge County worsening further to extreme drought.

Abnormally dry conditions persisting into July resulted in 332 square miles across northern Mower County realizing severe drought conditions by mid July. The rainfall deficit worsened during the second half of the month with 48 square miles across northeast Mower County being upgraded to extreme drought.

Abnormally dry conditions with rainfall totals 3 to 5 inches below normal for the month of June resulted in severe drought conditions developing across 394 square miles of northern Fillmore County in the beginning of July. While slight relief was realized into the middle of July from passing storm systems, dry conditions later in the month led to monthly rainfall finishing 2 inches below normal in spots. This resulted in 494 square miles, or 57% of Fillmore County experiencing severe drought conditions through July. Within this drought area, 97 square miles across northwest Fillmore County was upgraded to extreme drought conditions by mid July.

Abnormally dry conditions with monthly rainfall totals 2 to 5 inches below normal across Houston County for June resulted in severe drought conditions realized for 84 square miles, or 15% of Houston County in the beginning of July. While slight relief was realized into the middle of July from passing storm systems, July rainfall totals finished 2 inches below normal in spots. This resulted in 493 square miles, or 86% of Houston County in severe drought conditions by late July.

Abnormally dry conditions with monthly rainfall totals of 4 to 5 inches below normal in June across Olmsted County resulted in severe drought conditions developing across all of Olmsted County at the beginning of July. Through the rest of the month, ongoing abnormally dry conditions with rainfall totals 3 inches below normal in spots resulted in 476 square miles, or 73% of Olmsted County being upgraded to extreme drought conditions by mid July.

Abnormally dry conditions with monthly rainfall totals 3 to 5 inches below normal across Wabasha County in June resulted in severe drought conditions developing across 236 square miles of western Wabasha County in the beginning of July. Ongoing abnormally dry conditions throughout July with monthly rainfall nearing 2 inches below normal in spots resulted in 314 square miles, or 57% of Wabasha County in severe drought conditions.

Abnormally dry conditions with monthly rainfall totals 1 to 5 inches below normal across Winona County in June resulted in severe drought conditions developing across 172 square miles of western Winona County in the beginning of July. Ongoing anomalously dry conditions throughout July with monthly rainfall nearing 2 inches below normal in spots resulted in 264 square miles, or 42% of Winona County experiencing severe drought conditions by late July.

Highway 218 was closed due to flooding and Highway 9 east of Osage was closed since water topped the bridge. Widespread overland flooding continued across the county, which was described as a lake on Sunday June 8. Besides crop damage, many basements were flooded.

Flash flooding led to aerial flooding across much of the county.  Numerous roads and bridges remained closed, mainly in the northern part of the county.||In the Lime Springs area, the road to Lidtke park was damaged and water approached the top of the Lidtke Mill bridge.||Parts of Protivin was evacuated due to flood waters and ponding. Crops were also hit hard with too much standing water.

Excessive rainfall caused fairly widespread flash flooding across the county. Steep terrain enhanced the flash flood threat causing mud slides and damaged infrastructure. Numerous roads were washed out and bridges damaged. A mud slide at Camp Tahigwa Girl Scout camp near Dorchester trapped part of the staff, but no one was injured. In Dorchester, the Waterloo Creek flash flooded swamping several mobile homes or trailers and cars along Highway 76. Water swept through town very quickly trapping people on their cars and roof tops. There were three injuries as a result.

Rounds of thunderstorms produced flash flooding over large parts of the county. Many secondary roads were damaged including infrastructures. The Upper Iowa River also began to rise very quickly. Mudslides were also reported. The Protivin area near neighboring Howard County was also evacuated.

Flooding was extensive across the county from 4 to 5 inches of rain. Flooding along the Shell Rock river breeched a levee in Nora Springs on Sunday June 8th and flooding was extensive in Rockford, IA.  Perhaps as many as 60 secondary roads were washed out or closed. The Cedar River also began to rise quickly and ended up causing extensive damage through the county.||About 400 homes in Rockford had damage and roughly 20 others across more rural areas of the county.||Highway 18 was also closed east of Charles City due to damage from flood waters.

Highways 18 and 63 were closed in spots from flood waters. A Local Area Emergency (LAE) was issued for the county based on requests early Sunday morning June 8. Main roads were mostly open, but secondary and township roads were under water.  The Cedar River caused flooding in parts of Nashua where sand bagging efforts were unable to save a water main from breaking and cutting off the towns water supply.  Rainfall totals of 6 to 7 inches were reported during the weekend of June 7-8.

Several civil cmergency messages were issued for evacuations in the county. Nursing homes and residences in the lower areas on the west side of the city of Decorah were evacuated. Ponding of water in Decorah could not be stopped even with pumps running.  Many roads were closed in the county due to high water.||In Fort Atkinson, the supports to a train bridge gave way in addition to damage to Highway 24 near town.  Mudslides were also reported on County Road B32 between Fort Atkinson and Festina.||In Spillville, flood waters covered many of the streets and the waste water treatment plant.  Sand bagging efforts were haulted as flood waters condintued to rise. |The Turkey River flooded in Spillville and Fort Atkinson and damaged railroad bridges. The Highway 24 bridge over the Turkey was heavily damaged and had to be closed for repairs following the flood.
Numerous secondary roads were flooded. Over 5 inches of rain was reported for the weekend of June 7-8.

Many roads, mainly secondary, were washed out in the county. Rainfall totals of 5-7 inches were reported for the weekend of June 7-8 with widespread flood problems. About 2500 acres of crops were damaged.

Most secondary roads were either damaged or under water. Rainfall totals of 3 to 7 inches were reported during the weekend of June 7-8. About 4000 acres of farm land were impacted. Combined with flooding along the Turkey River, a total of 20 homes were destroyed, 9 with major damage, 15 with minor damage, and recovery costs easily into the millions.

River levels on the Upper Iowa River at Decorah and Bluffton crested at record levels.||Decorah crested at about 9 a.m. CDT on June 9 at 17.9 feet. The previous record crest was 15.2 feet on May 29, 1941. Flood stage at Decorah is 12.0 feet. Sand bagging was needed along the north end of town as water approached the Law Enforcement Center.  Several homes and roads were flooded on the east end of Decorah as well.||Bluffton crested at 15.49 feet about 2 a.m. on June 9. Flood stage at Bluffton is 14.0 feet.
The Upper Iowa River at Dorchester crested around 1 a.m. CDT on June 9 at a record level of 22.46 feet. The previous record crest was 22.2 feet on February 28, 1948. Flood stage is 14.0 feet.

The Cedar River at Charles City had a record crest at 25.55 ft, which occurred about 7:00 a.m. CDT on June 9. The previous record was 22.8 feet, which occurred on July 21, 1999. Flood stage is 12.0 feet. Of note, no river levels were available for a time from June 8-9 due to the river gage and gage house being completely underwater.||The two main traffic bridges in Charles City were closed, splitting the city in half. The walking suspension bridge in Charles City collapsed as well.  Immaculate Conception school took a direct hit as water topped all sand bagging efforts flooding the basement and first floor.  Many businesses also suffered damaged when water flowed into basements.  The fire department was evacuated as flood waters swamped that area of town.  Over 500 homes in Charles City were directly impacted.
The Turkey River at Garber had a major flood and crested at 29.1 feet around 11:30 a.m. CDT on June 10. The all-time record crest of 32.8 feet occurred on May 23, 2004. Flood stage is 17.0 feet.

The Turkey River at Elkader established a new record crest at about 6 a.m. CDT on June 10 of 30.9 feet. The previous record crest was 27.3 feet on June 15, 1991. Flood stage is 12.0 feet. The river rose again above flood stage from June 12 through June 14th cresting at 16.63 feet.

Abnormally dry conditions during the first half of July resulted in 100% of Juneau County being affected by at least severe drought conditions into the middle of July. Of this area, 233 square miles or 29% of southern Juneau County were upgraded to extreme drought by the middle of July. By the end of July, sporadic storms alleviated approximately 140 square miles of the extreme drought conditions, with 708 square miles or 88% of Juneau County still experiencing at least severe drought conditions.

Drier than normal conditions resulted in 100% of Adams County in at least severe drought conditions through July. Of this area, 77 square miles or 11% were upgraded to extreme drought conditions by mid July. Total monthly rainfall of 3 to 5 inches was around 1 inch below normal.

Abnormally dry conditions persisted into July, resulting in 83% of Monroe County, or 757 square miles, being affected by at least severe drought conditions. Increased rainfall through the middle of the month temporarily alleviated the severity of the drought before dry conditions returned. By the end of the month, at least 50% of the county, or 458 square miles, was back to at least severe drought, with the southeast corner worsening to extreme drought. Monthly rainfall departures from normal ranged from 2 inches below in the southern edge of the county to 2 inches above in the northern edge of the county.

Persistently dry conditions resulted in 99% of Crawford County being affected by at least severe drought conditions through July. Of this area, 256 square miles of eastern Crawford County, or 43% of the county, were upgraded to extreme drought during the middle of July. Total monthly rainfall of 2 to 3 inches in northern Crawford County was 2 inches below normal. Whereas, total monthly rainfall of 4 to 6 inches in southern Crawford County was an inch above normal.

Persistent abnormally dry conditions resulted in 100% of Vernon County being affected by at least severe drought conditions throughout most of July. Of this area, 319 square miles  of eastern Vernon County, or 39% of the county, were upgraded to extreme drought by mid July. Monthly precipitation totals bottomed out at 3 inches below normal in spots.

Abnormally dry conditions persisted through most of July and resulted in 100% of Richland County, or 590 square miles, being affected by at least severe drought conditions for the entire month. Conditions worsened to extreme across the entire county by mid July, but then some rainfall brought temporary slight alleviation in drought severity. Additional dryness later in the month returned 100% of Richland County to extreme drought conditions by the end of July. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2 inches below normal to 1 inch above normal in spots.

Abnormally dry conditions persisting into July resulted in 100% of Grant County being affected by at least severe drought conditions. Of this area, 487 square miles or 41% of northeast Grant County were upgraded to extreme drought by mid July. Increased rainfall slightly alleviated the severity of drought along the county's western edge during the second half of the month, whereas extreme drought conditions expanded slightly across northeast Grant County. Monthly precipitation totals ranged from 1 inch below to 1 inch above normal across the county.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 7 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought, worsened to extreme drought (D3) for nearly all of Adams County through August. By the end of August, extreme drought (D3) expanded, impacting roughly 76% of Adams County or 518 square miles. The United States Department of Agriculture declared Adams County as a contiguous natural disaster area due to the drought on August 17th.

The United States Department of Agriculture declared Grant County as a contiguous natural disaster area due to the drought on August 17th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 7 consecutive weeks of at least extreme drought (D3), expanded across all of Dodge County through September. By September 11th, less than a half inch of rain fell, more than inch below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture content was 50 to 70% below normal. A series of storms provided approximately 3 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, up to 2 inches above normal for the time period. These above normal rainfall totals resulted in downgrade of the extreme drought (D3) to severe drought (D2) for nearly all of Dodge County by the end of the month. The United States Department of Agriculture declared Dodge County as a contiguous natural disaster area due to the drought on September 7th and 22nd due to the ongoing drought.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 7 consecutive weeks of at least extreme drought (D3), worsened to exceptional drought (D4) for most of Fillmore County through the middle of September. By September 11th, approximately a half of an inch of rain fell across Fillmore County, more than inch below normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moisture content neared 70% below normal. A series of storms provided around 3 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, approximately 1 inch above normal for the time period. The above normal rainfall resulted in the downgrade of exceptional drought (D4) to extreme drought (D3) and the ongoing extreme drought (D3) to severe drought (D2) towards the end of September.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 10 weeks of at least severe drought (D2), worsened to exceptional drought (D4) for parts of Houston County through the middle of September. By September 11th, under a quarter of an inch of rain fell, resulting in top soil moistures 50% below normal. The consequential drought classification was upgraded to exceptional drought (D4) for nearly half of the county. A series of storms provided 3 to 5 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, approximately an inch above normal for the time period. These above normal rainfalls resulted in removal of exceptional drought (D4) towards the end of September as extreme (D3) and severe drought (D2) persisted for most of the area. The United States Department of Agriculture declared Houston County as a contiguous natural disaster area due to the drought on September 13th and 21st.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 7 consecutive weeks of at least extreme drought (D3), worsened to exceptional drought (D4) for nearly all of Mower County through the middle of September. By September 11th, approximately a half of an inch of rain fell across Mower County, which was half of normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moisture neared 70% below normal. A series of storms provided 2 to 3 inches of rainfall across Mower County during the second half of September, up to an inch above normal for the time period. As a result, exceptional drought (D4) was downgraded to extreme drought (D3) by the end of September, encompassing all of Mower County.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 9 consecutive weeks of at least extreme drought (D3), continued for all of Olmsted County through the middle of September. By September 11th, approximately a half of an inch of rain fell across Olmsted County, near 1 inch below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture content neared 70% below normal. A series of storms provided near 4 inches of rainfall across Olmsted County during the second half of September, up to 2 inches above normal for the time period. As a result, nearly all of the extreme drought (D3) was downgraded to severe drought (D2) across Olmsted County. The United States Department of Agriculture declared Olmsted County as a contiguous natural disaster area on September 1st and 7th. Broadcast media reported widespread impacts to both crops and outdoor tourism. Initial crop germination was delayed, reducing the size of apples and edibility of pumpkins without proper maturity. Crops near Rochester also suffered from the lack of water, with decreased yields and stunted growth.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 9 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), expanded to encompass nearly all of Wabasha County through the middle of September. By September 11th, under a tenth of an inch of rain fell across Wabasha County, more than an inch below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture dropped to 50 to 70% below normal. A series of storms provided around 5 inches of rainfall across Wabasha County during the second half of September, near 3 inches above normal in spots for the time period. This resulted in removal of severe drought (D2) towards the end of September for nearly all of Wabasha County, replaced by moderate drought (D1). The United States Department of Agriculture declared Wabasha County as a primary natural disaster area on September 1st. Reported impacts included a reduction in apple size at an orchard in Elgin as well as failed squash crops without necessary irrigation.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 9 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), expanded to all of Winona County at the start of September. By September 11th, under a half of an inch of rain fell across Winona County, which was 0.5 to 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture neared 50% below normal. A series of storms provided 3 to 4 inches of rainfall across Winona County during the second half of September, up to 2 inches above normal for the time period. This resulted in a downgrade of the severe drought (D2) to moderate drought (D1) for nearly the entire county towards the end of September. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture declared Winona County as a contiguous natural disaster area on September 1st, 7th, and 12th.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3), comprised of 7 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), worsened to exceptional drought (D4) for most of Allamakee County through the middle of September. By September 11th, under a quarter of an inch of rain fell across Allamakee County, more than 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moistures neared 50% of normal. By the middle of the month, all of Allamakee County was enveloped in exceptional drought (D4). A series of storms provided 3 to 6 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, about 1 to 4 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of exceptional drought (D4) by the end of September, but extreme drought (D3) persisted.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3) persisted through Chickasaw County, worsening to exceptional drought (D4) in the northeast part of the county by mid-September. By September 11th, less than a quarter of an inch of rain had fallen across Chickasaw County, which was more than 1.25 inches below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moistures reached 50 to 70% below normal. Farmers reported very poor conditions in southwestern Chickasaw and an earlier than normal harvest time. A series of storms provided up to 5 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, nearing 3 inches above normal in spots for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of exceptional drought (D4) by the end of September, while extreme drought (D3) persisted county-wide.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3) persisted across all of Clayton County and worsened to exceptional drought (D4) across the northeast part of the county by mid-September. Highly variable rainfall of a tenth of inch in the north to 1 inch in the south of Clayton County through September 11th was 0.5 to 1.5 inches below normal during this time. The resultant topsoil moistures were 50% of normal. A series of storms provided 1 to 3 inches of rainfall across during the second half of September, up to 1 inch above normal for the time period. The above normal rainfall resulted in removal of exceptional drought (D4) by the end of September, replaced by persistent extreme (D3) and severe drought (D2). This marked 11 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2) in Clayton County.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3) expanded across all of Fayette County by the end of September. Monthly rainfall totals near 3 inches were about 1 inch below normal. Resultant topsoil moistures were 50% below normal. Far southern Fayette County remained in severe drought (D2) through the middle of the month, only to be upgraded to extreme drought (D3) by late September due to continued below normal rainfall.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3) persisted through September for all of Floyd County. Highly variable monthly rainfall totals, from 1 inch in the west to 4 inches in the east were up to 2 inches below normal. Resultant topsoil moisture content bottomed out in the middle of the month to near 70% below normal.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3) worsened to exceptional drought (D4) for most of Howard County through the middle of September. By September 11th, under a quarter of an inch of rain fell across Howard County, more than 1 inch below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture was 50 to 70% below normal. A series of storms provided up to 4 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, 1 inch above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of exceptional drought (D4) by the end of September, while extreme drought (D3) persisted county-wide.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3) persisted through Mitchell County, worsening to exceptional drought (D4) for some through the middle of September. By September 11th, under a quarter of an inch of rain fell across Mitchell County, more than 1 inch below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture was 50 to 70% below normal. A series of storms provided up to 3 inches of rainfall during the second half of September. This rainfall removed the exceptional drought (D4) by the end of September, while extreme drought (D3) persisted county-wide.

Ongoing extreme drought (D3) worsened to exceptional drought (D4) for nearly all of Winneshiek County through the middle of September. By September 11th, up to a quarter inch of rain fell across Winneshiek County, up to 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture was 50 to 70% below normal. A series of storms provided 3 to 6 inches inches of rainfall during the second half of September, up to 3 inches above normal in spots during this time. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of exceptional drought (D4) by the end of September, while extreme drought (D3) persisted county-wide.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 7 consecutive weeks of extreme drought (D3), expanded in Adams County through September. Through September 11th, approximately a quarter inch of rainfall resulted in 50% below normal topsoil moisture. The increased longevity of abnormally dry conditions decreased water levels along the Wisconsin River to 10% of normal, marooning and killing many mussels along its banks. A series of storms provided 2 to 4 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, up to 2 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall lessened drought severity to extreme (D2) across the county. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture had declared Adams County as a primary natural disaster area on July 25th and a contiguous natural disaster area on August 10th and September 13th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 8 weeks of extreme drought (D3),  worsened to exceptional drought (D4) through the middle of September for nearly all of Crawford County. Rainfall totals under a a quarter of an inch through September 11th were up to 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moistures neared 50% below normal. Farmers in Gays Mills reported drastically increased irrigation to keep fruit trees and vines alive. The increased longevity of abnormally dry conditions also decreased water levels along the Wisconsin River to 10% of normal, marooning and killing many mussels along its banks. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rainfall up to 4 inches, which was up to 2 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of the exceptional drought (D4), though extreme drought (D3) continued for much of Crawford County through the end of September. The United States Department of Agriculture had declared Crawford County as a primary natural disaster area due to the drought on July 25th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 8 weeks of extreme drought (D3), continued through the middle of September for nearly all of Grant County. Highly variable rainfall totals ranged from a tenth of an inch in northern Grant County along the Wisconsin River Valley to more than 1 inch along the Iowa/Illinois border. The resultant departures from normal varied from near normal to 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moistures were 20 to 50% below normal. Volunteer observers reported variable crop conditions across Grant County, including some stunted to wilted crops. The need for increased irrigation to maintain healthy crops was apparent. The increased longevity of abnormally dry conditions also decreased water levels along the Wisconsin River to 10% of normal, marooning and killing many mussels along its banks. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided 2 to 4 inches of rainfall, up to 2 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of the exceptional drought (D4) from the northern part of the county, though extreme drought (D3) to severe drought (D2) continued for most of the county through the end of September. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture had declared Grant County as a primary natural disaster area on July 25th and a contiguous natural disaster area on August 17th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions continued through the middle of September for all of Jackson County. Rainfall totals under a tenth of an inch through September 11th were up to 1.5 inches below normal. Resultant topsoil moistures we 50% below normal. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rain resulting in up to 6 inches of rainfall, which was up to 3 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in only moderate drought (D1) to a sliver of severe drought (D2) across southern Jackson County by late September. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture declared Jackson County as a primary natural disaster area on September 13th and a contiguous natural disaster area on July 25th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 8 weeks of extreme drought (D3), expanded and continued through the middle of September for nearly all of Juneau County. Rainfall totals under a quarter of an inch through September 11th were 1.5 inches below normal. Resultant topsoil moistures were 50% below normal. The increased longevity of abnormally dry conditions decreased water levels along the Wisconsin River to 10% of normal, marooning and killing many mussels along its banks. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rain, resulting approximately 3 inches of rain. These rainfall totals were up to 2 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of nearly all of the extreme drought (D3) except for far southwest Juneau County, with severe drought (D2) persisting elsewhere through the end of September. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture declared Juneau County as a primary natural disaster area on July 25th and a contiguous natural disaster area on August 17th and September 13th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions classified by severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought continued through the middle of September for all of La Crosse County. Rainfall totals under a tenth of an inch through September 11th were up to 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moistures were 50 to 70% below normal. The Holmen and Onalaska Fire Departments issued burn and firework bans through Labor Day weekend due to the incredibly dry grasses. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rain, totaling 3 to 6 inches. These totals neared 3 inches above normal in spots for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of the extreme drought (D3), though moderate (D1) to severe (D2) drought persisted across the entire county through the end of September. The United States Department of Agriculture declared La Crosse County as a primary natural disaster area on September 13th due to the ongoing drought.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 8 consecutive weeks of at least extreme drought (D3), encompassed most of Monroe County at the start of September. Through September 11th less than a quarter of an inch of rain had fallen, resulting in 50% below normal top soil moistures. The result was expansion of the extreme drought (D3) as well as a sliver of southern Monroe County worsening to exceptional drought (D4). A series of storms provided 3 to 6 inches of rainfall during the second half of September, up to 4 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall removed the exceptional drought (D4) and shrunk the extreme drought (D3) area to southern Monroe County. Severe drought (D2) persisted across most of the rest of the county through the end of the month. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture declared Monroe County as a primary natural disaster area on July 25th and and a contiguous natural disaster area on September 13th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 8 weeks of at least extreme drought (D3), worsened to exceptional drought (D4) for parts of Richland County at the start of September. Rainfall totals under a quarter of an inch through September 11th were 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. The resultant topsoil moisture was 50% below normal. Volunteer observers reported widespread impacts to pastures and crops throughout Richland County. Reports included very limited pasture growth for grazing livestock, forcing farmers to acquire supplemental feed. The extremely dry soils created difficulties for ground work, as the clay became impenetrable. The increased longevity of abnormally dry conditions also decreased water levels along the Wisconsin River to 10% of normal, marooning and killing many mussels along its banks. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rain with totals nearing 3 inches in spots, up to 3 inches above normal for the time period. This above normal rainfall resulted in downgrading of the exceptional drought (D4) area to extreme drought (D3), with severe drought (D2) persisting across the remainder of the county through late September. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture declared Richland County as a primary natural disaster area on July 25th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions, comprised of 8 weeks of extreme drought (D3), worsened to exceptional drought (D4) across much of Vernon County through mid-September. Rainfall totals under a tenth of an inch through September 11th were near 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moistures were 50% below normal. Volunteer observers reported widespread very dry conditions, exacerbated along the Kickapoo River Valley with very low water levels. Some fire departments issued bans on fires and fireworks. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rain, totaling 3 to 6 inches across Vernon County. These totals neared 3 inches above normal in spots for the time period. The above normal rainfall resulted in downgrading of the exceptional drought (D4) to extreme drought (D3), with severe drought (D2) persisting elsewhere through the end of September. Due to the drought, the United States Department of Agriculture declared Vernon County as a primary natural disaster area on July 25th and a contiguous natural disaster area on September 13th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions persisted through the middle of September and resulted in severe drought (D2) impacting all of Trempealeau County. Rainfall amounts below a tenth of an inch through September 11th were near 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moistures were 50% below normal. Volunteer and farmer reports portrayed widespread impacts to crops, with corn, soybeans, and grass pastures reported to be wilted, dying, or very stunted. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rain with totals near 4 inches in spots, approximately 1 inch above normal for the time period. The severe drought (D2) eased to abnormally dry (D0) and moderate drought (D1) conditions by the end of September. The United States Department of Agriculture declared Trempealeau County as a contiguous natural disaster area on September 13th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions persisted through the middle of September and resulted in severe drought (D2) impacting nearly all of Buffalo County. Rainfall amounts under a third of an inch through September 11th were near 1.5 inches below normal for the time period. Resultant topsoil moisture bottomed out to nearly 50% below normal. Through the second half of the month, a series of storms provided multiple days of heavy rain, nearing 4 inch totals for much of Buffalo County, nearly 1 inch above normal for the time period. The severe drought (D2) eased to moderate drought (D1) by the end of September. The United States Department of Agriculture declared Buffalo County as a contiguous natural disaster area on September 7th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions persisted through the middle of September and resulted in at least severe drought (D2) across most of Taylor County. Through the first half of September, top soil moisture was 70% below normal. Rainfall totals during this time neared 1 inch below normal and resulted in severe drought (D2) expansion as well as extreme drought (D3) introduction in parts. Reported impacts included severely decreased crop yields, as well as a difficult harvest for cranberry farmers due to well below normal water levels. A series of storms during the latter half of the month provided approximately 3 inches of rainfall across Taylor County, up to an inch above normal for the time period. This resulted in only a portion of northern Taylor County remaining in severe drought (D2) by the end of September, with moderate drought (D1) persisting elsewhere. The United States Department of Agriculture declared Taylor County as a primary natural disaster area on September 13th.

Ongoing drier than normal conditions persisted through the middle of September and resulted in at severe drought (D2) impacting southwestern Clark County. A dry start to September resulted in top soil moisture bottoming out at 50% below normal. Rainfall totals during this time neared 1 inch below normal and resulted in the development of severe drought (D2). A series of storms during the latter half of the month provided 4 to 8 inches of rainfall across Clark County, near 4 inches above normal for the time period. Highest 24 hour total rainfall report from a volunteer observer was 2.44 between Willard and Thorp on the morning of the 23rd. This above normal rainfall resulted in removal of nearly of all the severe drought (D2) by the end of September, lessened to abnormally dry (D0) and moderate drought (D1). The United States Department of Agriculture declared Clark County as a contiguous natural disaster area on September 13th due to the drought.

Ongoing abnormally dry conditions with relative humidity values in the middle 20% range with increased wind gusts resulted in the rapid spread of a wildfire near the Necedah National Wildlife Refuge on September 4th. The fire had consumed 23.6 acres of land by the time it was 95 percent contained on September 8th.

Ongoing abnormally dry conditions, comprised of 14 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), eased slightly in Adams County through October. Multiple storms provided up to 3 inches above normal rainfall totals, slightly relieving the 6 inch rainfall deficit from initial severe drought (D2) issuance on June 27th to the start of October. As a result, severe drought (D2) retreated to the southern half of Adams County by the end of the month.

Ongoing abnormally dry conditions, consisting of 14 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), eased slightly in Juneau County through October. As a result, severe drought (D2) retreated to the southern half of Juneau County by the end of the month.

Ongoing abnormally dry conditions, consisting of 15 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), eased slightly through October in Vernon County. Ongoing abnormally dry conditions, consisting of 15 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), eased slightly through October. Ongoing abnormally dry conditions, consisting of 15 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), eased slightly through October. Ongoing abnormally dry conditions, consisting of 15 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought (D2), slightly eased in Richland County through October. Ongoing abnormally dry conditions, consisting of 15 consecutive weeks of at least severe drought, eased through October. The Kickapoo River at Ontario crested at a record level of 21.96 feet about 9:45 p.m. CDT on June 8. The previous record crest of 18.85 feet occurred on March 14, 2007. Flood stage is 18.0 feet. The river levels actually dipped just below flood stage around 7:00 a.m. CDT on June 8th before rising very quickly back up. Unoffically Ontario picked up 9.84 inches of rain over the weekend.  Water swamped the intersection of Highways 33 and 131 and backed up into town.  The village's baseball field and nearby parks were submerged along with nearly 3 feet of water into some businesses.

The Kickapoo River at La Farge reached a record crest of 15.88 feet around midnight on June 9. The previous record crest of 14.92 feet occurred on July 1, 1978. Flood stage is 12.0 feet. Unofficially La Farge picked up 6.39 inches of rain over the weekend.  The southern and eastern parts of town were hardest hit.

The Kickapoo river at Viola reached a record crest of 21.25 feet around 5 a.m. on June 9. The previous record crest of 21.0 feet occurred on July 1, 1978. Flood stage is 14.0 feet.  Water was over bridge railings on the bridges.
The Kickapoo River at Readstown crested at a record level of 19.65 feet around 7 a.m. on June 9. The previous record crest of 19.08 feet occurred on July 21, 1951. Flood stage is 12.0 feet.

The Kickapoo River at Soldiers Grove reached the second highest crest on record of 21.21 feet around 5 a.m. CDT on June 9. The all-time record crest of 21.63 feet was established on July 22, 1951. Flood stage is 13.0 feet.  About 50 to 60 homes were flooded.  The village park and Highway 131 bridge was badly damaged.

The Kickapoo River at Gays Mills reached a record crest of 20.44 feet around 10 a.m. CDT on June 9. The previous record crest of 19.80 feet occurred on July 2, 1978. Flood stage is 13.0 feet.  About 175 homes and businesses were flooded.
The Kickapoo River at Steuben crested at a record level of 19.15 feet around 2 a.m. CDT on June 10. The previous record crest of 18.0 feet occurred on July 3, 1978. Flood stage is 12.0 feet.
Trees were blown down onto Highway 35.
Several trees were blown down along Highway 61 between Boscobel and Fennimore, as well as along County Highway P.  Trees were also blown down in Fennimore, especially around the cemetery.

Flooding was reported over the southern half of the county. Roads that were closed due to high water included Highway 63 in Spring Valley and County Highway 15. A rainfall total of 7.25 inches was recorded for the weekend of June 7-8 in Harmony where over 100 basements flooded. There were nearly 300 homes impacted in the county along with contaminated or collapsed wells.  Other county roads closed due to high water included 17, 12, 30, and 8.  In Preston, 12 business were affected and the city waste water treatment plant was flooded.  Some evacuations were needed in Preston, along with Lanesboro.

Very heavy rain led to flash flooding through much of the county. A rainfall total of 7.18 inches was measured 3 miles southwest of Reno. The bridge over Clear Creek was reported damaged and unsafe for use. In addition, highway 26 was closed due to mudslides. County Highways 5, 23, 31 and 249 were closed due to high water and washouts.

Widespread flooding forced the closure of virtually all roads across the county. Several civil emergency messages were sent by request of county officials for evacuations in mainly the southern half of the county. An estimated 9300 acres of corn and 5400 acres of beans were lost. There were massive mudslides in some parts of the county, just like in August 2007. Debris backup was common against area bridge supports.
Numerous roads were closed due to high water, especially over the south part of the county near the Minnesota-Iowa state line. Creeks ran very high in Austin area.
Street flooding was reported in Winona.

The Root River went into flooding due to the heavy rains during the weekend of June 7-8.  The South Branch of the Root River at Preston crested at 941.67 feet on June 9, which was the third highest crest on record. Flood stage is 937.0 feet.  At Lanesboro, the South Branch of the Root River reached 14.17 feet with a flood stage there of 12 feet.
Hardest hit by flash flooding were locations in the southern part of the county, including the communities of Adams and Lyle.
Flash flooding impacted a large part of the county, especially the southern half. High water was reported over Highways 30 and 44. Many area creeks rose very rapidly and caused infrastructure damage.
Many area roads near Warrens, WI were closed and covered with water and debris. Most notable closures were in the area of US HWY 12 and CO HWY EW. Water Depth of 3 to 4 feet was noted in some places.
Variable hail sizes of up to 1 inch were reported east of Warrens. Leaves and branches were taken off trees.

The Cedar River in Austin reached a crest of 22.4 feet at the waste water treatment plant and 21.4 feet 3 miles south of Austin. Both of these crests occurred on June 12 and were the third highest on record. Flood stage at the waste water treatment plant is 15.0 feet and 11.0 feet 3 miles south of Austin. In addition, Turtle and Dobbins Creek near Austin crested at 13.74 feet and 18.95 feet respectively on June 12, which were both the second highest crests on record. All-time record crests were 14.77 feet at Turtle Creek, 25.0 feet at the waste water treatment plant and 23.26 feet 3 miles south of Austin, all of which occurred on September 16, 2004. Dobbins Creek all-time record crest was 19.18 feet on July 10, 2000.||Sections of Interstate 90 were closed from flood waters along the Cedar River.

The South Branch of the Baraboo River at Hillsboro reached a crest of 14.91 feeet around Midnight CDT on June 8th, only to reach a second crest of 16.17 feet around 9 p.m. CDT later that day.  This was a record crest for this location.  The previous record crest was 15.6 feet on June 29, 1990. Flood stage is 13.0 feet.

This tornado crossed the Mississippi River from Winona County, Minnesota, damaged trees at Merrick State Park and in the bluffs east of Highway 35. Falling trees at the state park heavily damaged a guest restroom that was designated as a storm shelter, crushing in the roof.

This stronger EF1 tornado leveled trees and powerlines along an intermittent track that was mixed with downburst winds. The tornado was overtaken by a downburst, which caused pockets of tree and outbuilding damage for another 7 miles.

The Turkey River through northern and northeast Fayette County experienced a record flood. At Eldorado, the river crested at a record level of 22.11 feet about 9 a.m. CDT on June 9. The previous record crest was 19.6 feet in May 2004. Flood stage is 12.0 feet. Flood stage levels were also exceeded at Clermont.||Damage in Eldorado was surprisingly minimal with flood waters only impacting a few homes directly near the river on the north side of the village. Further southeast though several bridges and roads were damaged or destroyed as debris would pile up along bridge supports and running water flowed over highways. A large bridge north of West Union, called the Huntzinger Bridge, on County Road W42 was broke apart in two sections. County Road B40, known as the river road was also closed and heavily damaged.||In Clermont, the Turkey River heavily damaged the Skip-A-Way Campground on the southwest edge of town. River levels quickly rose out of their banks and swept across many of the camp sites heavily damaging at least 50 of them. Water also flowed into a holding pond and busted a new opening back to the Turkey River leading to even more infrastructure damage. Luckily no one was killed or injured.||In Elgin, local officials decided to breach the road on the north side of the river, allowing flood waters to spill into a nearby rural home to protect the downtown area.

Throughout the entirety of September and through October 29th, only 1 to 2 inches of precipitation fell in Grant County. This 2 to 5 inch deficit for this period resulted in the development of severe drought across southern Grant County by mid-October. Severe drought conditions ended in Grant County by October 31st when roughly 2 to 4 inches of rainfall fell across the county in the final week of October.

Throughout the entirety of September and through October 29th, only 0.5 to 1 inches of precipitation fell in Fayette County. This 5 to 7 inch deficit for this period resulted in the development of severe drought by mid-October. Severe drought conditions ended in the county by October 31st when roughly 1 to 2 inches of rainfall fell across the county in the final week of October.

Throughout the entirety of September and through October 29th, only 0.2 to 1 inches of precipitation fell in Chickasaw County. This 5 to 7 inch deficit for this period resulted in the development of severe drought by mid-October. Severe drought conditions ended in the county by October 31st when roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of rainfall fell across the county in the final week of October.

This weak tornado began just south of the Dodge and Mower County line before moving into Dodge County.

This strong EF-2 tornado began on the northeast side of Stewartville resulting in damage to several homes. The tornado then moved northeast through rural areas of Olmsted County while being highly visible on MNDOT cameras and from Rochester. This tornado eventually crossed I-90, hitting a semi-trailer and injuring the occupant, before moving northwest of Simpson. A farmstead near Simpson took a direct hit from the tornado where a single-wide manufactured home was rolled and farm outbuildings were destroyed. The tornado continued northeast into a neighborhood along Marion Road where several homes were rendered uninhabitable due to a collapse of their exterior walls and roof. Numerous other residences sustained window, roof, and outbuilding damage as well. The tornado continued through this neighborhood before dissipating along Timberidge Court between Rochester and Marion. Two more individuals were also injured in this area while sheltering in their home from the tornado.

This EF-1 tornado began in northeast portions of Rochester resulting in minor roof damage to a couple of homes before moving northeast through rural portions of Olmsted County, damaging trees and a few electrical poles before moving into Wabasha County.
This tornado moved into Wabasha County from Olmsted County and damaged outbuildings and one residence along its path before dissipating near the intersection of County Road 2 and 550th Street.

This strong EF-2 tornado began in rural portions of Olmsted County east of Viola where it damaged some farm outbuildings as it moved northeast. As the tornado approached the Wabasha County line, it strengthened and significantly damaged a farmstead, removing large sections of the roof and other portions of the home and outbuildings. It then continued northeast into Wabasha County.
This tornado continued into Wabasha County from Olmsted County where it damaged one residence, some farm outbuildings, power poles, and trees before dissipating near 230th avenue.

This intense EF-3 tornado began near Blank Hill Road where it quickly intensified before damaging three homesteads near highway 88 south of Cream. The most significant damage was to one home where much of the exterior walls were collapsed onto the foundation forming the basis for the EF-3 rating. Other homes and outbuildings sustained significant damage near highway 88 as well. The tornado continued northeast and weakened slightly where additional homes and outbuildings sustained damage before the tornado lifted near County Road X just northeast of Montana.

This tornado began west of Blair and tracked northeast resulting in damage to outbuildings, trees, and minor damage to one residence. The tornado continued into the hills north of Blair as its damage path became more intermittent, eventually dissipating west of the Trempealeau/Jackson County line.
This tornado started just west of Interstate 94 and damaged some trees before moving east into Jackson County.

This tornado continued from northeast Trempealeau County where it crossed Interstate 94, moving northeast into far northwest Jackson County where it caused roof damage to two residences and damaged a significant number of trees.

This tornado developed near the Black River before moving eastward through areas south of Hatfield. Most of the damage from this tornado was to trees, with limited damage to any infrastructure. The tornado then dissipated just northeast of the intersection of County Road K and Old Highway 54.

This tornado developed northwest of Saratoga and was witnessed by multiple individuals as it tracked northeast, damaging one outbuilding. The tornado also rolled a truck with the driver sustaining minor injuries. The tornado then dissipated southeast of the intersection of 70th street and Kent Avenue.

A local fire department provided a video of a brief tornado southeast of Postville. This tornado is not known to have encountered any damage indicators. Therefore, no numerical rating was able to be assigned to this tornado.
This tornado began in rural far eastern Vernon County where it caused minor damage to a residence and damaged some trees before moving into Juneau County.

This tornado moved into Juneau County from Vernon County where it intensified quickly and hit a residence at EF-3 intensity, destroying the home's above ground level. As the tornado moved east, it produced significant tree damage before weakening in intensity as it approached State Road 80, where it damaged a few more homes and several outbuildings. The tornado continued northeast, dealing intermittent tree and structural damage at EF-1 intensity along its path until it dissipated just west of Overgaard Road.

A tornado caused damage on the north and northeast side of the city of Austin. Specific reports included minor tree damage, as well as debris blown into fences and bent poles on the northwest side of Austin. Several power poles were snapped off or bent along Highway 218 on the north side of the city. Several metal work buildings were heavily damaged along 243rd St, along with numerous trees and some minor roof damage to nearby homes. Large debris, such as metal dumpsters, were tossed large distances. There was straight-line wind damage noted south of the tornado path, or along Highway 218 and 4th St NW. Several homes had minor damage, with numerous trees blown over or sheared off along 236th and 237th Street directly north of downtown Austin. There was considerable damage done in Todd Park, including athletic equipment, small buildings and hundreds of trees toppled and uprooted. The north side of the park, including the northern softball fields had the most damage. There was also considerable tree damage along 21st St NE or 555th Ave, which continued into the Austin Country Club. Minor damage was noted about a half mile east of the Austin airport and about 2 miles southeast of the airport. One minor injury was reported when a man sustained scrapes and bruises when he took shelter in a shed that rolled over twice.
