A total of 5 inches of rain fell in Brownsdale between 2 p.m. and 5 p.m. CST.
Amateur radio operators reported that 2.18 inches of rain fell in in about 15 minutes in Rochester.
Water covered parts of U.S. Highway 52 at the exit for 75th Street NW in Rochester.
A total of 5.70 inches of rain fell in a two hour period at the Mississippi River Lock and Dam 5A near Fountain City.
Heavy rain produced standing water that covered parts of County Highways D and OO south of Strum and County Highway B and Call Road south of Osseo. The roads were closed until the water receded.
Heavy rains produced some standing water over U.S. Highway 12 and State Highway 27 northeast of Black River Falls.
A carnival tent was blown over at the Taylor County Fair.
Lightning struck a house on the northeast side of Rochester. The strike melted a hole through a gas line, ignited the gas causing a small fire.
Locally heavy rains in Rochester flooded several city streets dislodging some manhole covers.
Heavy rains pushed Turtle Creek out of its banks from the 16th into the 17th. The creek crested over a foot above the flood stage at 11.74 feet.
Flooding along the Shell Rock River occurred in Rockford from heavy rains that fell over portions of southern Minnesota and north central Iowa.
Several trees were blown down on a farm east of Disco.

Farms in the rural Town of Irving lost some livestock sheds and had outbuildings damaged. Several fields of corn were also flattened but it was thought that most of the corn would recover with little crop loss.
A cabin at the Wisconsin Christian Youth Camp was damaged by strong thunderstorm winds.

Lightning struck a tree and started a fire in the attic of the nearby house. The damage from the fire was limited to the attic, but smoke damage to bedrooms on the upper level made the house uninhabitable until repairs were made. Firefighters were on the scene for about 2 hours.
Some corn was flattened by the high winds near Waltham.
Heavy rain created flooding in Austin and along parts of Interstate 90. A few motorists became stranded in the high water.
A wind gust of 61 mph was measured near Grand Meadow.
Water was over State Highway 30, County Road 13 and some streets in Kasson.
An automated weather observing system on the north side of Rochester measured 4.53 inches of rain during the late morning and afternoon.
A total of 4.11 inches of rain was measured during the late morning and afternoon.
Widespread street flooding was reported in Rochester with some streets under 1 to 2 feet of water.
Lightning struck a house causing a small fire.

Lightning struck a one hundred thirty-nine year old church and caused a fire. Firefighters from 3 communities battled the fire for several hours. Major damage occurred to the roof and steeple but falling debris and water damaged the exposed interior. The building was later declared a total loss with estimates of $1.2 million to replace it.
A couple of trees were blown down in St. Charles.
A couple of power lines were blown down in Hawkeye.
A large tree was blown down in West Union.

Numerous trees were blown down or uprooted in Wadena. Some of the trees went down on power lines. A two inch diameter flag pole was bent over and some cornfields were flattened. The high winds caused a school bus to slip off the road south of West Union with some of the students on board receiving a few bumps and bruises.
Water six to eight inches deep covered some streets in Fayette. The thunderstorms dumped 2.76 inches of rain in a very short time to produce the flooding.
Trees were blown down near the Mississippi River.
Trees were blown down in a rural area.
Spotted near County Road MM west of Greenwood from a distance.
Up to golf ball sized hail fell in Thorp.

Two people were directly injured and there was an indirect loss of life from an EF2 tornado that tracked across the east central sections of Clark County near Chili. The death occurred when an oxygen machine stopped working due to a power outage caused by the tornado. The tornado was on the ground for just over 7 miles and destroyed four homes, damaged at least 19 others, destroyed four barns and 15 outbuildings with numerous other farm buildings damaged. One farmer lost several specialty birds including 12 peacocks and 16 guinea hens. Around 1500 residents across Clark County were without power after the storms moved through. Damages from the tornado are estimated to be around $1.5 million.
Half dollar sized hail fell in Neillsville.
Lightning struck a tree causing it to split apart and fall onto the side of a nearby house.
Lightning struck a satellite dish on the top of house and traveled through wires into the attic igniting a fire. The fire damaged one room in the house and the garage.
A homeowner sustained minor injuries after lightning sparked a small garage fire. The nearby house only sustained minor smoke and water damage.
Lightning from an early morning thundestorm struck a house in Westby causing the brick chimney to explode.
A semi truck was blown over on State Highway 9 near Cresco.
An estimated wind gust of 70 miles per hour occurred in Chester blowing down several power lines.
A tree was blown down on a house and several other trees and light poles were damaged in Osage.
Numerous branches and small trees were blown down in and near Decorah.
Several large trees were blown down across State Highway 139 near Kendallville. In addition, a tree went down on a house northwest of Kendallville on County Road A14.

Widespread tree damage and power outages occurred in Riceville. Also, two light poles were blown down at the Rasmussen High School football field. One of the poles fell on a set of portable bleachers.
A building roof and several grain bins were damaged, a shed destroyed and 70 power poles blown down along Jade Avenue five miles west of Lime Springs.

Heavy rain caused water to go over County Road M in the township of Chelsea, created minor street flooding in Medford and filled ditches with water north of Medford. 2.90 inches of rain was reported in the city of Chelsea.
A cooperative observer measured four inches of rain that fell in a 4 to 5 hour stretch.
Numerous trees were blown over, a shed was destroyed, a barn roof damaged and wind turbine blades bent in or near Stacyville.
Trees were blown down along State Highway 16.
An estimated a wind gust of 60 miles per hour blew down several branches two miles northeast of Newburg.
An estimated 60 miles per hour wind gust occurred four miles southwest of Winona.
An estimated a 60 mile per hour wind gust occurred near Pickwick.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down near Brownsville.
Large tree branches were blown down in Spring Valley along with a few trees over County Road 1.
Trees and power lines were knocked down in Lyle and some penny sized hail also fell. One of the trees fell on a garage causing some minor damage.
Several trees were blown down along State Highway 35 between Centerville and Trempealeau.
An estimated 60 mile per hour wind gust occurred in Galesville.

Several trees and power lines were blown down in the city of La Crosse. One tree went down on an apartment building on South 33rd Street with several trees down in the vicinity of the Shelby ball fields.
The automated weather observing equipment at the La Crosse Municipal airport measured a wind gust of 63 miles per hour. A 62 mph gust was also measured at the same time in Onalaska.
An estimated wind gust of 60 miles per hour occurred in West Salem.
An estimated wind gust of 70 miles per hour occurred three miles northeast of Westby which knocked down a pine tree and caused damaged to a house.
A roof was blown off a house in Chaseburg.
Numerous trees were blown down with power outages in Stoddard and Genoa.

Several trees and power lines were blown down in and near Coon Valley. Especially hit hard, was the Norskedalen Nature & Heritage Center where more than 20 trees went down and several windows were broken by wind blown walnuts.
An estimated 60 mph wind gust blew down several large trees along County Road I four miles east of Cataract.
Numerous jack pine trees were snapped off, a 14 inch diameter tree blown down, and a large oak tree split four miles south of Norwalk.
An estimated 60 mile per hour wind gust occurred in Tomah.
A tree was blown down on a home with other trees down on power lines on Newport Road near Cashton.
Trees were blown down on power lines causing power outages in Wilton.
A tree was blown down on a mobile home three miles southwest of Norwalk.
Large tree branches were blown down which caused siding and roof damage in Oakdale.
Several trees were blown down near Sandstone Estates with one falling on trailer.
Numerous trees were blown down and other trees were snapped off from three miles southwest of Necedah to three miles southeast of Necedah.
Several six inch diameter trees were blown down near Castle Rock Park.
Trees and power lines were blown down four miles north of Friendship. One of these trees fell on a vehicle on State Highway 21 at the entrance of Roche-A-Cri State Park.

Trees and power lines were blown down across portions of Adams County. The downed trees blocked roadways and fell on top of homes and cars. According to the emergency manager, it appears that Preston Township in the central part of the county, was hit the hardest with downed trees.
A house was destroyed by a fire started by a lightning strike.
At least 31 apple trees were blown down at the Maple Ridge Orchard.
The roof was blown off of a grain elevator. Numerous trees were also blown down, some of which blocked city streets.
An estimated wind gust of 60 miles per hour occurred in Strawberry Point.
A few trees including one large tree were blown down on County Road D south of Platteville.
An estimated a wind gust of 60 miles per hour occurred in Mount Hope which blew down some small tree branches.

Several trees were blown down in Charles City and a chimney was knocked off a house. This damage occurred with an extended period of sustained northwest winds of 20 to 30 mph with some gusts that approached 50 mph during the late morning and afternoon of the 29th.

Widespread corn and bean fields were flattened across Mitchell County. The USDA estimated that 500 acres of corn were destroyed while 81,000 acres suffered a 60% yield loss. Almost 8,600 acres of beans suffered a 10% yield loss. Total crop losses were estimated to be in excess of $41 million. The U.S. Department of Agriculture issued a natural disaster designation for this damage.

Numerous corn fields were flattened across Howard County. The USDA estimated that almost 3200 acres of corn were destroyed while 16,000 acres suffered a 25 bushel per acre yield loss. Total crop losses were estimated to be around $7.5 million. The U.S. Department of Agriculture issued a natural disaster designation for this damage.
An above ground pool was flipped over and several tree branches were blown down.
Trees were blown down southwest of Reno including an 18 inch diameter cottonwood.
A semi truck was blown over on U.S. Highway 63 north of Davis Corners and sustained  minor damage.
Several large grain bins were buckled by the high winds.
Numerous trees were blown over in Lime Springs.
An estimated 60 mph wind gust occurred in Boscobel blowing down some small tree branches.
Up to golf ball sized hail fell just east of Monroe Center.
The hail covered the ground.

A field fire occurred southwest of Austin when a combine caused a soybean field to start on fire. The fire spread toward a residential area but fire fighters were able to extinguish the blaze before any evacuations were needed. The combine was lost to the fire.

A fire started in a combine and quickly spread to the field being harvested. The fire was being fanned by 30 mph wind gusts and was able to jump a road and start another field on fire. No damage occurred to the combine, but around 2 acres of corn was lost in the blaze. Farmers assisted firefighters in putting the fire out by spreading manure and tilling the dirt around the perimeter of the fire.
Severe drought conditions developed across Dodge County because of a persistent lack of precipitation since May 2011. Local officials were not issuing any burning permits or allowing any campfires.

Only around 0.25 inches of precipitation fell across Dodge County during November. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Moderate fire danger conditions existed and burning permits were needed in areas that had less than 3 inches of snow on the ground.

Severe drought conditions developed across parts of Mower County because of a persistent lack of precipitation since May 2011. Moderate fire danger conditions developed and burning permits were needed where ever there is less than 3 inches of snow around the burn area.
Accumulating light snow created icy roadways and caused a fatal accident on State Highway 13 approximately four miles west of Edgewood.

Only around 0.75 inches of precipitation fell across Dodge County during December. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Low fire danger conditions exist, however, burning permits were required where ever there was less than 3 inches of snow around the burn area.

Around an inch of precipitation fell across Mower County during December. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during November 2011. Low fire danger conditions exist, however, burning permits were required where ever there was less than 3 inches of snow around the burn area.
A volunteer observer estimated 6.5 inches of snow four miles east of Wilton.
A volunteer observer estimated 8 inches of snow one mile south of Mauston.

A woman was injured in an early morning accident near Whitehall after she lost control of her vehicle on an ice covered road. Light freezing rain had occurred during the early morning hours of December 3rd.
Light freezing rain created icy roadways across Floyd County. One fatality occurred from a single car accident near Charles City.

Six people were injured, two of them seriously, in a two vehicle accident south of Arcadia during the late afternoon of December 3rd.  Three to four inches of snow had fallen creating slippery roads resulting in the accident. The two serious injuries were the result of the occupants being ejected from the vehicle.
Estimated wind gusts of 60 miles per hour created sporadic power outages across Mitchell County.
Estimated wind gusts of 60 miles per hour created sporadic power outages across Floyd County.

Between a half and one inch of precipitation fell across Dodge County during January. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Low fire danger conditions exist, however, burning permits were required where ever there was less than 3 inches of snow around the burn area.

Between three quarters of an inch and an inch of precipitation fell across Mower County during January. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during November 2011. Low fire danger conditions exist, however, burning permits were required where ever there was less than 3 inches of snow around the burn area.

After a morning of steady snowfall, a short period of heavy snow occurred in the early afternoon with all the snow ending by late afternoon. Much of Grant County received 6 to 7 inches of new snow, but with minimal problems. The winds were light through the day and little or no drifting snow occurred. The Grant County Sheriffs office reported a total of 13 vehicle slide offs or accidents that occurred during the period of snowfall.

A person died after being involved in a two vehicle accident near Spring Valley that occurred in dense fog. The automated weather observing equipment at the Preston airport reported a visibility of a quarter mile or less from 7 p.m. February 2nd until 10 a.m.

Between one and two inches of precipitation fell across Dodge County during February. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Fire fire danger conditions were low, however, burning permits were required where ever there was less than 3 inches of snow around the burn area.

Between one and two inches of precipitation fell across Mower County during February. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Fire danger conditions were low, however, burning permits were required where ever there was less than 3 inches of snow around the burn area.

Observers across the extreme southern portions of Clayton County measured 7.4 inches of snow in Strawberry Point and 6.8 inches in Edgewood. The remainder of Clayton County received much less snow as a tight gradient existed with amounts quickly diminishing to 1 to 2 inches.

Observers across the extreme southern portions of Grant County measured 5.2 inches of snow in Sinsinawa and 5 inches near Cassville. The remainder of Grant County received much less snow as a tight gradient existed with amounts quickly diminishing to 1 to 3 inches.

A wide range of snowfall amounts occurred across Clark County. The northern half of the county received heavy snow with amounts ranging from 6 to 10 inches. The southern half of the county received less snow as temperatures became warm enough for the snow to mix with or change over to rain. There was also a short period of some freezing rain and sleet during the morning and afternoon of the 29th. The highest reported snowfall total was 10.3 inches two miles north of Owen.

An extended period of moderate to heavy snow fell across all of Taylor County. By the time the snow ended, much of county was covered in a foot or more of snow. There was also a short period of some freezing rain and sleet during the morning of the 29th. The highest reported snowfall total was 17 inches at Medford.

One fatality occurred from a two vehicle accident near Westgate. The accident occurred on snow covered roads while snow was falling. Much of Fayette County received 4 to 5 inches of snow with only minor problems occurring. The Fayette County Sheriffs office reported at least 10 vehicle slide offs or accidents occurred during the period of snowfall.

Between one and two inches of precipitation fell across Dodge County during March. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Fire danger conditions increased to very high by the end of the month and burning permits were required.

Between three quarters of an inch and a inch and a half of precipitation fell across Mower County during March. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Fire danger conditions increased to very high by the end of the month and burning permits were required.
Hail that ranged in size from three quarters of an inch up to an inch fell for a couple of minutes south of Jump River.
Power poles were blown down in Waukon.
A barn was lifted off its foundation and landed on a house southwest of Eitzen while power poles and lines were blown down in Eitzen.
The automated weather observing equipment at the Rochester International airport measured a wind gust of 58 mph.

Winds ripped the lids off four 50,000 bushel galvanized steel bins and pushed them over. An empty 30,000 gallon fuel tank was also toppled. Some grain semi-trailers were also likely damaged when the bins landed on them.

Between two and three inches of precipitation fell across Dodge County during April. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Because of the rain and the spring green up, fire danger conditions decreased to low by the end of the month but burning permits were still required.

Between two and three inches of precipitation fell across Mower County during April. This was not enough to alleviate the severe drought conditions that developed during October 2011. Because of the rain and the spring green up, fire danger conditions decreased to low by the end of the month but burning permits were still required.

Severe drought conditions developed across the western half of Olmsted County because of a persistent lack of precipitation since May 2011. By the end of the month, fire dangers were reported as low, but burning permits were still required.

Severe drought conditions developed across the southwestern portion of Wabasha County because of a persistent lack of precipitation since May 2011. By the end of the month, fire dangers were reported as low, but burning permits were still required.

Almost 2 inches of rain fell across Dodge County over the first part of May. This rain, combined with the rain the fell at the end of April, was enough to end the severe drought that began in October 2011.

Almost 2 inches of rain fell across Mower County over the first part of May. This rain, combined with the rain the fell at the end of April, was enough to end the severe drought that began in October 2011.

Over 2 inches of rain fell across Olmsted County over the first part of May. This rain, combined with the rain the fell at the end of April, was enough to end the severe drought that began in April 2012.

Over 2 inches of rain fell across Wabasha County over the first part of May. This rain, combined with the rain the fell at the end of April, was enough to end the severe drought that began in April 2012.
Pea to nickel size hail covered the ground across far northwest Dodge County.
Golf ball size hail was reported along with an estimated wind gust of 50 miles per hour on County Road 10 two miles west of Wabasha.
A wind gust to 74 mph was measured in the city of Wabasha which blew trees down and caused power outages.
A Minnesota Department of Transportation automated weather observing equipment measured a wind gust of 64 miles per hour near Kellogg.
Trees were blown down and power outages occurred in Alma. In addition, one inch hail covered the ground, damaged vehicles and a cracked at least one windshield.
Pea to quarter size hail covered the ground in Strum.

Thunderstorms impacted the central portion of Trempealeau County near and in Blair.  Nearly every structure in Blair was either damaged or destroyed by the hail or wind, with broken windows, siding or roof damage. The Blair-Taylor high and elementary schools suffered major damage to their roofs. A 25 to 30 unit mobile home park was evacuated after several mobile homes were moved off their foundations and ruptured natural gas lines. Numerous trees and power lines were blown down with power outages lasting up to 16 hours.
Trees were blown down and power outages occurred in Taylor.
Trees were knocked down at the intersection of 8th and Johnson Streets in Charles City.
An estimated wind gust of 60 miles per hour occurred in Decorah.
An estimated wind gust of 70 mph knocked down trees in Harmony. In addition, A NWS Storm Survey found a 20 inch tree branch snapped at the high school.
Trees were knocked down blocking State Highway 43 near Bratsberg.
Trees were blown down onto parts of State Highway 76 between Houston and Caledonia.
Dime to quarter size hail fell in Big Flats.
Power lines were blown down in the town of Shelby. More than 440 people were without power when a tree fell on a power line.
National Weather Service employee reported a couple of trees and six inch diameter branches were blown down north of Holmen.
A picnic table was flipped over and pea size hail fell in Galesville.
An estimated wind gust of 60 miles per hour occurred in Holmen.
Hail ranging in size from pennies to quarters fell just west of Marble Rock.
Trees were knocked down and covered a road in Saint Ansgar. Also, a roof was blown off a wine processing facility.
Up to golf ball sized hail fell just southwest of Charles City.
Penny to nickel sized hail fell in Charles City.
Quarter to golf ball sized hail fell at the intersection of County Road B and State Highway 82.
Pea to dime sized hail fell in Muscoda.
Lightning struck and damaged a county communications tower. The lightning strike blew out the surge protectors damaging the power supply.

Apple orchards across Wabasha County estimated losses of 20 to 80 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Winona County estimated losses up to 90 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Houston County estimated losses up to 90 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Clark County estimated losses up to 100 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Crawford County estimated losses of 20 to 25 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Pear and plum crops were also hit hard while damages to tart cherry orchards ranged from little loss up to 80 percent. The first blooming of strawberries were completely loss but subsequent bloomings are doing fine. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across La Crosse County estimated losses up to 80 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Trempealeau County estimated losses of 90 to 100 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Jackson County estimated only minimal losses, possibly up to 10 percent, from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

A brief tornado, along a line of storms, damaged numerous barns, grain buildings, outbuildings, and some homes along and just northeast of U.S. Highway 18 north of Hawkeye, IA.  Most of the damage was EF0 but peak wind speeds and described damage briefly reached EF1.
The hail covered the ground.
A lot of penny to nickel sized hail fell with some quarter size stones mixed in.
A roof was blown off an older building along County Highway A about a mile west of the Marathon County line. At the next farm, located just to the northwest, some trees were blown down.
A number of trees were blown down in Frankville.

Apple orchards across Allamakee County estimated losses up to 80 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Clayton County estimated losses up to 80 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Winneshiek County estimated losses up to 80 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.

Apple orchards across Mitchell County estimated losses up to 50 percent from freezing temperatures that occurred after the start of the growing season. Exact crop damage numbers will not be known until the fall harvest.
Lightning struck and caught a house on fire northwest of Melrose. The house was totally destroyed by the fire.

Lightning hit a power substation in Rochester causing power outages and damage to the substation. About 1,800 residences and businesses in the Eyota, Marion, Pleasant Grove, Stewartville and south Rochesters areas lost power.

Lightning struck a tower located next to a house with the power surge traveling through some cables to enter the house. The house, located north of Dodge Center, did not immediately catch on fire, but by the time the fire was reported and fire fighters arrived, the attic was fully engulfed in flames. The house is considered a total loss.
Lightning struck a house and caused a fire. The house sustained minor fire damage to the roof and attic while the second floor was damaged by heat, water and smoke.
Utility poles were blown down on Main Street in Fountain. Several trees were also blown down in the area with one landing on a small grain truck and another on a house causing damage to the roof.
A wind gust of 64 mph was measured by spotters in Harmony.
Several trees were blown down 2.5 miles west of Harmony.
Trees were blown down in Goodview. In nearby Minnesota City, several trees were also blown down landing on some houses causing some roof damage.
Widespread tree damage occurred in Winona.
A cluster of maple trees near Wilton was blown down from strong gradient winds.
Several trees were blown down in Arcadia.
An estimated 60 mph wind gust occurred along with marble sized hail north of Whitehall.
Numerous trees and powerlines were blown down near the intersection of County Highway H and Miller Avenue.
An estimated wind gust of 60 mph occurred along with 1 inch hail just north of Hannibal.
Trees were blown down along Starr Road south of Lynn.
Trees were blown down at the intersection of State Highway 95 and Riviera Ave.
Trees were blown down at the intersection of Resewood Ave. and Colby Factory Road.
Trees were blown down at the intersection of County Highways P and N.
Trees were blown down at the intersection of Pine Road and Hiline Ave.

Several trees across Clark County were blown down from strong gradient winds. A home sustained roof damage northwest of Spencer and at least one tree was blown down onto power lines in the Greenwood area.
Trees were blown down at the intersection of County Highway C and Hammond Road.

Just east of Waukon, a two foot diameter tree was twisted off at it base and fell onto a house. Three semi-permanent farm buildings were lifted and moved by the wind. One of these buildings was destroyed upon impact with the ground.

Two barns were blown down between Castalia and Ossian. One of these barns was a 114 foot by 283 foot freestall barn under construction. On the same farm, another calf barn was partially destroyed and three cattle sheds were completely destroyed. One cow was killed, 55 acres of corn was sheared off by the wind and 50 acres of alfalfa was destroyed.
In addition to the quarter sized hail, 1.73 inches of rain fell in about a half hour ending at 11:15 a.m. south of Claremont.
The automated weather observing equipment at the Rochester International airport measured a wind gust of 69 mph.
Over two inches of rain fell in about a half hours time near Eyota.
Locally heavy rain produced some street flooding in the city of La Crosse that included the intersection of U.S. Highways 14/61 (Mormon Coulee Road) and Losey Boulevard.
The hail ranged in size from one inch up to golf ball in Big Flats.
Several trees were blown down near the intersection of State Highway 23 and County Road B.

Grain bins, sheds and a portion of the roof on a hog barn were damaged by thunderstorms winds on a farm north of Lewiston. At another farm, a small barn was destroyed with some of the debris landing on a car parked nearby.

A semi and trailer were blown over causing State Highway 93 to be closed for about two and half hours north of Elk Creek. The driver of the semi sustained minor injuries but refused medical treatment.
Heavy rains pushed the Black River out of its banks in Black River Falls. The river crested about a half foot above the flood stage during the early morning of May 7th.
In approximately an hour and a half, 2.7 inches of rain fell in Big Flats.
A brief funnel cloud was sighted west of Marble Rock.
In about two and a half hours, 3.5 inches of rain fell in West Concord.

Locally heavy rains across the north half of Wabasha County produced mudslides on U.S. Highway 61, caused water to go over County Road 15 at the intersection with U.S. Highway 63 and flooded basements.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Whitehall.
Several mobile homes and trees were damaged in Arcadia.
A two foot diameter tree and power lines were blown down in Frankville.
Trees were blown down on Old Stage Road three miles west-northwest of Waukon.
Trees were blown down on Dug Road three miles northeast of Waukon.
Numerous trees were blown down in Elgin.
Trees were blown down just south of Claremont.
A trained spotter reported numerous trees down and a rotating wall cloud near Wasioja.
A semi was blown over between Dodge Center and Kasson on U.S. Highway 14.
Trees were blown down in Genoa.
A wind gust of 62 miles per hour was measured at the KTTC television studio.
Several large tree branches were blown down in Elgin.
Several trees and power lines were blown down producing power outages north of a line from between West Concord and Dodge Center east to the Dodge/Olmsted county line.
Near Theilman, a two foot diameter tree was snapped in half and a barn was completely destroyed.
A barn roof was damaged by thunderstorm winds near Byron.

Numerous trees and power lines were blown down north of a line from Rock Dam Campground to Loyal. In Rock Dam Campground, a tree fell on a camper but no injuries occurred. Poppel River Road in the northwest part of the county was closed for a half  mile stretch due to downed trees and scattered power outages were reported in the northern parts of the county.

As a severe thunderstorm moved across the northern section of Wabasha County it dropped large hail damaging around 30 percent of the county's alfalfa crop. On farms near Lake City, up to 80 percent of the alfalfa crop was damaged, one cow was killed and irrigation systems were twisted by the wind.

Severe to extreme drought conditions developed across Grant County because of a persistent lack of precipitation. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency due to drought for much of the southern half of the state, including Grant County. Affects of the drought include damaged crops, pastures that have stopped growing, river flows that were less than 20 percent of normal on the Wisconsin River, falling ground water levels and high to extreme fire dangers resulting in burning bans. In late July, the U.S. Dept. of Agriculture declared Grant County a natural disaster area. Also in late July, enough rain had fallen that the Wisconsin DNR lifted the burning ban across Grant County.

A severe thunderstorm that tracked across central Trempealeau County caused crop damage to around 150 farms. Around 2000 acres of alfalfa were destroyed along with almost 1100 acres of corn. Most farmers were able to replant the lost corn acres.

Severe to extreme drought conditions developed across Richland County because of a persistent lack of precipitation. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency due to drought for much of the southern half of the state, including Richland County. Affects of the drought include damaged crops, pastures that have stopped growing, river flows that were less than 20 percent of normal on the Wisconsin River, falling ground water levels and high to extreme fire dangers resulting in burning bans. In late July, the U.S. Dept. of Agriculture declared Richland County a natural disaster area. Also in late July, enough rain had fallen that the Wisconsin DNR lifted the burning ban across Richland County.

Severe drought conditions developed across Adams County because of a persistent lack of precipitation. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency due to drought for the entire state, including Adams County. Affects of the drought include damaged crops, pastures that have stopped growing, river flows that were less than 20 percent of normal on the Wisconsin River, falling ground water levels and high to extreme fire dangers resulting in burning bans. In addition, blue-green algae  growing on area waterways was responsible for one illness after a person water skied and swam in Lake Petenwell. In late July, the U.S. Dept. of Agriculture declared Adams County a natural disaster area. The Wisconsin DNR lifted the burning ban on July 30th.

Severe drought conditions developed across Juneau County because of a persistent lack of precipitation. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency due to drought for the entire state, including Juneau County. Affects of the drought include damaged crops, pastures that have stopped growing, river flows that were less than 20 percent of normal on the Wisconsin and Lemonweir Rivers, falling ground water levels and high to extreme fire dangers resulting in burning bans. A slow moving tornado formed on the edge of a passing severe thunderstorm between Patch Grove and Bloomington. The tornado was mainly confined to one landowner near Hickory and Maine Roads in rural Grant County.  Several outbuildings, a barn, and the home were demolished or heavily damaged.  Trees on the property were also sheared off or blown over.  Considering the roof was torn off and several walls were down or damaged, the tornado was rated an EF2 but it's possible the slow movement allowed the tornado to remain nearly stationary long enough to cause worse damage. Interviews by local residents and video evidence suggests the tornado may have moved to the northwest at times as well.

A log home was completely destroyed by a fire that was started by a lightning strike. Fire crews were first called to the area around 330 a.m. but found no evidence of a fire and left. They returned to the scene around 5 a.m. to find the home completely engulfed in flames. Three fire departments battled the fire for over 4 hours. Local officials estimated the value of the home and contents at just over $200,000.

A house on the southeast side of Rochester was struck by lightning which started a fire in the attic. The fire was quickly brought under control but the lightning strike created a serious electrical problem in the house and two firefighters received minor shocks but were not injured.

One woman was killed and another seriously injured from vehicle accidents that occurred in thick smoke from a wildfire. In the first accident, one vehicle was rear ended by another. While the drivers where standing between the two vehicles inspecting the damage, a third vehicle slammed into the back of one of the vehicles from the first accident pushing it into the women. A 57 acre wildfire in the Necedah National Wildlife Refuge was responsible for the smoke that closed a 10 mile portion of State Highway 173 both Saturday Sept. 29 and Sunday Sept. 30th. The fire was started by a hawk that got tangled in power lines and was battled by crews from the Warrens Fire Department, Wisconsin DNR and U.S. Fish and Wildlife.

A rainfall reported of 2.9 inches was reported by the public northwest of Rochester.

The combination of several rounds of rain and melting snow caused the Black River in Black River Falls to go above flood stage three times between April 9th and April 20th. The first round of flooding occurred between the 9th and 12th with a crest of 51.02 feet on the 10th. The second round of flooding occurred on the 15th and 16th with a crest of 49.25 feet on the 16th. The final round of flooding occurred on the 19th and 20th with a crest of 49.15 feet on the 19th. Flood stage at Black River Falls is 47 feet.

The combination of several rounds of rain and melting snow caused the Black River near Galesville to go above flood stage three times between April 11th and April 21st. The first round of flooding occurred between the 11th and 14th with a crest of 13.35 feet on the 12th. The second round of flooding occurred between the 17th and 19th with a crest of 12.49 feet on the 18th. The final round of flooding occurred on the 20th and 21st with a crest of 12.58 feet on the 21st. Flood stage at Galesville is 12 feet.

The combination of melting snow and several rounds of rain caused the Trempealeau River in Dodge to go above flood stage three times between April 1st and April 19th. The first round of flooding occurred on the 1st and 2nd with a crest of 9.21 feet on the 1st. The second round of flooding occurred between the 5th and 14th with a crest of 10.74 feet on the 11th. The final round of flooding occurred between the 16th and 19th with a crest of 9.95 feet on the 17th. Flood stage at Dodge is 9 feet.

After several rounds of rain, the Upper Iowa River near Dorchester went above flood stage two times between April 10th and April 15th. The first round of flooding occurred on the 10th and 11th with a crest of 14.58 feet on the 11th. The second round of flooding occurred on the 15th with a crest of 14.5 feet. Flood stage at Dorchester is 14 feet.

After several rounds of rainfall, the Kickapoo River at Readstown went above flood stage two times between April 10th and April 12th. The first round of flooding occurred on the 10th with a crest of 11.06 feet. The second round of flooding occurred on the 11th and 12th with a crest of 11.34 feet on the 12th. Flood stage at Readstown is 11 feet.
After several rounds of rain, the Kickapoo River at Viola went out of its banks on April 10th and 11th. The crest was 15.05 feet on the 11th. Flood stage at Viola is 14 feet.
Flooding that began in late March along the Zumbro River at Zumbro Falls ended on the 1st. This flooding closed County Road 68 just southeast of Zumbro Falls.

The combination of snow melt and several rounds of rain caused the Whitewater River in the Whitewater State Park to go in and out of flood stage three times between April 4th and April 14th. The first round of flooding occurred on the 4th with a crest of 13.63 feet. The second round of flooding occurred on the 10th with a crest of 13.89 feet. The final round of flooding occurred on the 14th with a crest of 13.72 feet. Flood stage in the Whitewater State Park is 13.5 feet.
County Road 81 was closed near the entrance to Kruger State Park due to flooding along the Zumbro River.
East Fork Road in the Town of Komensky was closed due to flooding caused by an ice jam on the East Fork of the Black River.
Hawk Island Road in the Town of Manchester was closed from April 11th into May due to flooding and high water on the Black River.
Stetzer Road in the Town of Melrose was closed from April 8th into May due to flooding and high water on the Black River and Germann Valley Creek.
County Highway VV south of North Bend was closed from April 9th to April 23rd due to flooding and high water on the Black River.
A lightning strike destroyed one of three blades on a wind turbine near Dexter.
County Highway P in the Town of Stark was closed from April 10th into the 11th due to flooding along the Kickapoo River.

Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 7 and 17 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported total was 17.2 inches in Dodge Center, which established a new Minnesota state record for a two day snow total in the month of May. A new Minnesota state record for a one day snow total in the month of May also occurred at Dodge Center when 15.4 inches fell on the 2nd.
Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 7 and 14 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported total was 14.0 inches in Grand Meadow.

Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 8 and 16 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported total was 16.6 inches west of Rochester. Over 100 trees were damaged in one Rochester cemetery.

Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 2 inches in the far eastern part of the county to as much as 13 inches of snow on the western edge.  The highest reported total was 12.9 inches east of Spring Valley.
Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 8 and 15 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported total was 15.8 inches near Reads Landing.
Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 1 and 11 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported total was 11.5 inches north of St. Charles.
Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 4 and 10 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported total was 10 inches in Charles City.
Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 7 and 13 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported total was 13 inches in Osage.
Volunteer and COOP observers reported between 3 and 8 inches of snow across the county. The highest reported was 8.3 inches west of Mondovi.
The automated weather observing equipment at the Charles City airport measured a wind gust of 58 mph.
Three sheds were destroyed with some of the debris wrapped around power lines and a 2x6 was driven into another building on farms southwest of Mitchell.
Quarter sized hail was reported in Charles City.
Lots of quarter sized hail fell and covered the ground along State Highway 9 just west of Osage.
A barn was blown down along with numerous large trees north of Nora Springs. One of the trees fell on a house.
A barn was blown over west of Osage killing 5 head of cattle that were inside the barn at the time.

Heavy rain produced wide spread flash flooding across much of Mitchell County. Numerous roads around Stacyville were under water by early evening and sand bagging occurred along the Little Cedar River. U.S. Highway 218 was closed by flooding between Osage and St. Ansgar and State Highway 9 was closed east and west of Osage. West of Osage, two culverts were washed away, causing a section of Highway 9 to collapse. A total of 22 roads were closed, 6 to 8 bridges washed out and approximately 90 percent of the gravel roads across the entire county were covered with water. Damage to the roads was estimated to be around $4.5 million. In addition to all the road damage, a railroad bridge north of St. Ansgar was also washed out. The Stacyville fire department reported between 6 and 7 inches of rain had fallen during the mid and late afternoon hours. The heavy rains also took out about 15 percent of the county's corn crop.
Numerous garages and buildings were damaged across New Hampton. Power lines and approximately 100 trees were also blown down.
A grain elevator was damaged in Fredericksburg.
Some houses in Calmar had siding and shingles ripped off and numerous trees were snapped off.
Trees were blown down in Postville.
Trees were blown down in Waukon.
Numerous roads in Nora Springs were under water. Dancer and Echo Avenues in the northwest corner of the county were closed as flood waters from Flood Creek covered the roads.
Trees were blown down east of Waukon.
Around 30 large pine trees were blown down south of Stewartville.

The automated weather observing equipment at the Rochester International Airport measured a wind gust of 60 mph. There were also reports from the northwest side of Rochester of power outages and debris blown onto area streets. Some trees were blown down with at least one landing on a car breaking the back window. Around 5,000 customers in Rochester lost power because of the storm.
Power lines and trees were blown in St. Charles. The strong winds also damaged a building of a local agricultural business.

Damage to buildings occurred from about 2 miles north of St. Charles to 4 miles north of St. Charles. Large trees were blown down along with a pole barn and corn cribs. Six foot long sections of tin were ripped off other buildings and some one inch hail also fell.
Water from a branch of the Upper Iowa River was flowing over State Highway 56 west of Le Roy.
Trees were blown down and one inch hail fell in Lewiston. One of the large trees blown down fell across U.S. Highway 14 with both lanes blocked for about 15 minutes.
Wind gusts from a line of thunderstorms caused a semi truck to jack knife on Interstate 90 southwest of Lewiston.
Wind gusts of 65 to 74 mph occurred south of Lewiston.
Vehicles and a deck were damaged when large tree branches landed on them.
A 62 mph wind gust occurred in Winona.

Sandbagging occurred in Adams and County Roads 4 and 7 near Adams were closed as water from several branches of the Little Cedar River were out of their banks. Flood waters covered much of the business district in Adams with little damage occurring to those that were able to sand bag. For those that didn't, water reached into the buildings creating minor damage.

Flood waters from Rose Creek inundated Jellystone Campground east of Austin. A pedestrian bridge was severely damaged. The majority of the campers and RVs in the park were moved to safety, but a few vehicles did suffer some water damage. Highway shoulders in the area were washed out and some secondary roads were closed by the high water.
Trees and power lines were blown down south of Cochrane.
Around a dozen power poles were blown down in Gilmanton.
One inch hail and wind gusts to 50 mph were reported in Eleva.
Trees were blown down in Lancaster.
Golf ball sized hail fell east of Potosi.
Wind gusts of 60 mph occurred in the vicinity of the Lone Rock airport.
One inch was reported north of Ossian.
A 60 mph wind gust was reported in Nashua.
The automated mesonet observing equipment near Ionia measured a wind gust of 62 mph.
A wind gust of 63 mph occurred in New Hampton.
Sandbagging occurred in Protivin after heavy rain pushed Bohemian Creek out of its banks.
A farm shed was blown down, a grain bin was twisted and torn, windows were broken and machines were damaged on a farm east of Oelwein.
A pole barn was damaged and numerous trees were knocked down from east of Garnavillo to the Wisconsin state line in the Mississippi River east of Clayton.

Heavy rain caused Goddard Creek to go out of its banks with water covering part of State Highway 24 just outside of Fort Atkinson. In and around Calmar, water was over several county roads and State Highway 24. Street flooding in Calmar also occurred along with water getting into the basements of some houses. Widespread street flooding from heavy rain occurred in Decorah. In about an hour and 45 minutes, 3.5 inches of rain fell in Fort Atkinson, the COOP observer in Calmar received 3.43 inches and the public reported 3.5 inches of rain in Decorah.

Heavy rain produced street flooding and caused water to go into several basements in Lawler. Widespread flooding also occurred over the eastern sections of the county and numerous streets were flooded in New Hampton.

Heavy rain overwhelmed small streams east of Edgewood causing water to go over State Highway 3. Numerous other streams over the southern half of the county also went out of their banks causing water to flow over roads. The COOP observer in Edgewood reported 4.1 inches of rain.
Numerous fields were underwater north of Oelwein from heavy rain.
Numerous streets were under water in Charles City from excessive rain. The storm sewers were not able to keep up with the rain as it fell.
A roof was damaged and tree limbs blown down by a 68 mph wind gust in Cherry Grove. Just south of town, a storage shed was destroyed and shingles were blown off a garage.
A tin roof was blown off a structure in Fountain.
The automated weather observing equipment at the Preston airport measured a wind gust of 58 mph.
Heavy rain pushed Badger Creek out of its banks causing water to flow over State Highway 76 north of Caledonia.
Trees were blown down near County Road F south of Arcadia.
Just south of Whitehall, a pole barn was blown down, other large structures were damaged and numerous tree limbs were blown onto the highway.
Quarter sized hail fell in Merrillan.
Heavy rain caused street flooding to occur in the city of La Crosse and also caused some manhole covers to pop off.
A small tornado crossed the Mississippi River from Clayton County going through a campground north of Bagley before dissipating.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Prairie du Chien.
Buildings and trees were damaged along County Road SS southeast of Viroqua. Another shed near Viroqua was also damaged.
A funnel cloud was sighted southwest of Muscoda.
South of Richland Center, buildings and trees were damaged.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Wonewoc.
A wind gust of 65 mph occurred south of Necedah.
Trees were blown down along County Road G and State Highway 23 southeast of Plainville.
Heavy rain caused water to spread over several roads in Bagley as the drainage system was not able to keep up the rain. Streams in the area were running very high.
In Le Roy, 1.1 inches of rain fell in about 30 minutes.
A 60 mph wind gust occurred in Mt. Hope.
In West Salem, 1.79 inches of rain fell in 45 minutes.
In Fairbank, 3.2 inches of rain fell.
In Edgewood, 4.5 inches of rain fell.
Southeast of the city of La Crosse, 2.3 inches of rain fell.
In West Salem, a total of 2.69 inches of rain fell.
A wind gust of 70 mph occurred just south of Lancaster.
Trees were blown down west of Gotham near the Grant County line.
Trees and power lines were blown down west of Big Flats.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Adams.
Trees and power lines were blown down southwest of Grand Marsh.
An estimated wind gust of 60 mph occurred southeast of Garnavillo.
An estimated wind gust of 65 mph occurred west of Viroqua.
An estimated wind gust of 60 mph occurred south of Eastman.
Trees were blown down in the city of La Crosse.
Golf ball sized hail fell between Kellogg and Plainview.
Quarter sized hail fell and there was also a 57 mph wind gust south of Rochester.
Quarter sized hail covered the ground in Predmore.
Golf ball sized hail fell southeast of Rochester.

Quarter sized hail just outside of Le Roy.

Heavy rains pushed Deer Creek out of its banks causing water to go over roads in the vicinity of Carpenter.
In St. Ansgar, 4.43 inches of rain was reported.
The automated mesonet observing equipment in Osage measured 3.84 inches of rain.
Funnel clouds were sighted in Calmar.
Funnel clouds were visible in Decorah.
Heavy rains caused several small streams that feed the Maquoketa River to go out of their banks south of Arlington. At least three roads were closed due to washouts or water over the road.
The automated mesonet reporting equipment in the town of Fillmore reported 2.39 inches of rain.
The COOP observer in Grand Meadow reported 2.21 inches of rain.
The automated mesonet reporting equipment in Dover reported 2.52 inches of rain.

Heavy rains across the western sections of Fillmore County caused numerous roads to be closed and basement flooding to occur in Spring Valley. The high water stranded several heads of cattle in the Wykoff and Fillmore areas.
In La Crescent, 2.23 inches of rain fell.
Trees were blown down across U.S. Highway 14/61 in Westby.
Funnel clouds were sighted near Muscoda.
Funnel clouds were sighted near Richland Center.
A 58 mph wind gust occurred in Mt. Sterling.
Quarter sized hail fell north of Fountain City.
The driver of a vehicle was able to escape before it sank after attempting to drive through flood waters from a local creek in Waucoma.
A grain bin was blown over on a farm south of Mitchell.
A metal building was blown over and trees uprooted on a farm southwest of Mitchell.
On a farm near Spring Valley, 38 trees were either uprooted or snapped off.
Trees were blown down in Rollingstone, temporarily blocking traffic on South Main Street.

Heavy rains caused the Little Cedar River to go out of its banks east of Charles City. The flood waters damaged a railroad bridge causing an 80 car train to derail into the river. The two employees on the train were rescued without sustaining any injuries. A small amount of diesel fuel from one of the locomotives and ethanol from a tank car leaked into the river.
Up to half dollar sized hail fell in Marion.
Lightning struck a tree on the southwest side of Rochester causing a nearby natural gas line to start on fire. Firefighters cooled the fire until the utility company clamped off the gas line.
Lightning struck a house on the southeast side of Rochester causing a fire in the attic. The fire was quickly put out but extensive damage was done to the roof and attic.
Runoff from heavy rains pushed the Black River out of its banks in Black River Falls. The river crested over two feet above the flood stage at 49.31 feet.
Runoff from heavy rains pushed the Trempealeau River out of its banks at Dodge. The river crested over a foot above the flood stage at 10.34 feet.
Runoff from heavy rains pushed the Whitewater River out of its banks in the Whitewater State Park. The river crested less than a half foot over the flood stage at 13.9 feet.
Runoff from heavy rains pushed the South Branch of the Root River out of its banks in Preston. The river crested just over a foot above the flood stage at 938.07 feet.
Runoff from heavy rains pushed the Root River out of its banks near Houston. The river crested a foot and a half above the flood stage at 16.52 feet.
Runoff from heavy rains pushed Dobbins Creek out of its banks in Austin. The creek crested a foot and a half above the flood stage at 13.01 feet.
Runoff from heavy rain pushed the Cedar River out of its banks in Charles City. The river crested over seven and a half feet above the flood stage at 19.52 feet.
Runoff from heavy rain pushed the Upper Iowa River out of its banks near Dorchester. The river crested almost four feet above the flood stage at 15.86 feet.
Runoff from heavy rain pushed the Upper Iowa River out of its banks near Dorchester. The river crested almost a foot above the flood stage at 14.99 feet.
Runoff from heavy rain pushed the Turkery River out of its banks in Elkader. The river crested almost four feet above the flood stage at 15.86 feet.
Runoff from heavy rain pushed the Turkey River out of its banks in Garber. The river crested almost five and a half feet above the flood stage at 22.47 feet.
Runoff from snow melt and heavy rain that moved down the Mississippi River, pushed the river out of it banks at McGregor. The river crested less than a half foot above the flood stage at 16.29 feet.
Stetzer Road in the Town of Melrose was closed starting in April until May 16th due to flooding and high water on the Black River and Germann Valley Creek.
Hawk Island Road in the Town of Manchester was closed starting in April until May 9th due to flooding and high water on the Black River.
A funnel cloud was sighted northwest of West Concord.
A tornado briefly touched down west of West Concord. The tornado was not on the ground long enough to produce any damage.
A funnel cloud was spotted southeast of Waucoma.
Funnel clouds were sighted near New Hampton.
A funnel cloud was spotted near Dexter.
Another funnel cloud was spotted near Dexter.
Trees were blown down between Marquette and McGregor with at least one of these trees going down on a power line. Other trees were blown down just north of Marquette on to State Highway 76.
A funnel cloud was sighted in Guttenberg.
An estimated 60 mph wind gust occurred in Port Andrew.
Locally heavy rain caused some street flooding in Boscobel.
Ping pong ball sized hail was reported south of Whalan.
Trees were blown down just northwest of Charles City.
A wind gust of 59 mph was measured in Nora Springs which blew down numerous trees and power lines with one tree landing on a garage.
Quarter sized hail fell in Oran.
Trees were blown down northwest of Marble Rock.

Heavy rain across Floyd County caused flash flooding to occur at numerous locations. Water covered some roads near Floyd causing some washouts. Numerous roads became impassable with washouts in and near Nora Springs and roads on the east side of Charles City also became covered with water. The Shell Rock River topped the levee in Nora Springs washing away a 40 foot section of the levee.
Heavy rain caused the Little Cedar River to rise rapidly and produce flooding that closed roads east of Orchard.
Small wispy funnel clouds from some showers were sighted southwest of Eyota.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Mondovi.
A pontoon boat was flipped upside down on Lake Onalaska.
Trees and large branches were blown down in the city of La Crosse.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Westby.
Locally heavy rain caused street flooding to occur in several locations across the city of La Crosse.
The automatic weather observing equipment at the Boscobel airport measured a wind gust of 58 mph. Trees were blown down in Boscobel from this wind gust.
Roads in Prairie du Chien were closed as runoff from locally heavy rains produced flooding.
Several trees were blown down in Muscoda.
Locally heavy rain produced rapid runoff and flash flooding at several locations across the county.
Locally heavy rain produced street flooding in Chaseburg, Westby and Viroqua.
A minor mud slide just south of Genoa covered part of State Highway 35.
A couple of power poles were struck by lightning in Holmen.
Some minor flooding occurred south of Wacoma as just over 2 inches of rain fell in an hour.
Locally heavy rain caused some water to go over State Highway 35 near Patch Grove.
Several trees were blown down in Platteville.
Quarter sized hail was reported east of Oelwein.
Several roads were closed northwest of Oelwein as locally heavy rain produced some flash flooding. Almost two inches of rain fell in about an hour.

The tornado began as a waterspout in the marsh waters just off the main channel of the Mississippi River southeast of Winona, Minnesota, but on the Wisconsin side.  White spray could be seen for some distance as the waterspout pulled up water into the funnel.  The tornado then moved onshore in the Trempealeau Wildlife Refuge and knocked down numerous trees for nearly a half mile.  Water plants were found on the refuge roads suggesting they were thrown some distance.
Very heavy rain fell at such a fast rate that the sewer stations in Waukon were not able to keep up with the rain and as a result, flooding occurred around the city.
At least two large trees were blown down on roads and a shed was blown off its foundation on the northwest side of Rochester. On the southwest side of the city, widespread power outages occurred.

Very heavy rain produced flash flooding across the northeast part of Grant County. |In Boscobel, numerous houses became surrounded by water with evacuations needed, most streets were flooded and cars were under water. 650 homes were impacted by the flood waters with two dozen families displaced. County Roads M and S near Boscobel were impassable due to high water and several other county roads between Blue River and Fennimore were covered with water and impassable. Portions of County Road C southwest of Woodman were under water. The flooding washed out sections of State Highway 133 outside of Woodman and Blue River. Debris was washed down Glass Hollow and Dry Hollow Creeks where it became lodged across railroad bridges in Bagley producing flooding in the town. The railroad tracks through Woodman were washed out. Flooding debris blocked some roads around Patch Grove. 54 canoeists had to be rescued from the Wisconsin River because of rising water.
Power lines were blown down in Eyota.
Trees were blown down east of Lewiston along U.S. Highway 14.
Locally heavy rains produced street flooding on the northwest and southeast sides of Rochester.

Locally heavy rain produced flash flooding across portions of Crawford County. Water covered roads in the Steuben area. Mudslides occurred that closed U.S. Highway 61 and State Highway 60 in the southeast part of the county. Other mudslides closed State Highway 35 between Lynxville and Prairie du Chien. Numerous streets and basements were flooded in Prairie du Chien. Homes and businesses were evacuated in Gays Mills and Stueben ahead of the expected flooding along the Kickapoo River.
A house in Holmen was struck by lightning. The electrical box, some windows and the roof were damaged.
Locally heavy rain produced flash flooding across portions of Allamakee County. Paint Creek was pushed out of it banks with the water covering a road northeast of Waterville.

Locally heavy rain produced flash flooding in numerous low lying areas across the county with many secondary roads under water. A campground outside of McGregor suffered extensive damage with a bridge and part of a road washed out, a bathroom facility destroyed and numerous picnic tables washed away. Some permanent camp foundations were also washed away and four campers had to be evacuated.

Locally heavy rain produced flash flooding across mainly the far southwest part of Richland County. Knapp Creek and numerous other small streams were out of their banks with County Road F flooded south of Excelsior.

Heavy rain produced flash flooding across the southwest half of Richland County. Numerous streams were forced out of their banks with water reported over County Highway JJ between Gotham and Lone Rock, State Highway 56 near Gillingham and the intersection of County Highways O and OO near Richland Center. Mud slides closed County Highway O northwest of Gotham. State Highway 60 between Gotham and the Crawford County line southwest of Westport was closed by a mudslide with other damage reducing the road to one lane at times.

Heavy rain caused mud slides to occur closing State Highway 35 in several places north of Prairie du Chien to the Vernon County line just south of De Soto. High water covered State Highway 131 between Wauzeka and Stueben.

Heavy rain produced flash flooding across the southwest sections of Vernon County. High water went over State Highway 162 near Chaseburg. Flash flooding was reported around Genoa where a boulder the size of a dump truck slid off a bluff and on to State Highway 56. Streams that drained into the Kickapoo River around Readstown were out of their banks.

Very heavy rain caused widespread flash flooding across a good portion of Houston County. Roads around the town of Houston became covered with water and impassable. Rapidly rising water along Riceford Creek caused a campground to be evacuated. A mudslide occurred just outside of Spring Grove. Numerous other roads around the county sustained damage, including County Highway 27 which had a complete section washed out. State Highway 16 east of Houston, State Highway 76 between Caledonia and Houston and County Highway 43 along with numerous other county roads were closed along with at least 20 township roads. In the western part of the county, one vehicle was swept off a road and the driver had to be rescued and at least three campers and a 73 foot mobile home were washed down Crystal Creek. In Hokah, the Root River rise high enough to top the levee requiring a local auto dealership to move about 60 cars to save them from the water. The flooding washed away a gravel road and two walking bridges at Camp Winnebago near Caledonia.
Heavy rain caused a mud slide southeast of Minneiska. The mud slide took down some trees, one of which went across U.S. Highway 61 and blocked a lane of traffic.

Mudslides occurred over the eastern section of the county from Lansing to north of Harpers Ferry covering portions of County Road X52. Other flash flooding occurred over much of the county. A campground in the Yellow River State Forest had to be evacuated with 80 campers moved to community building in Harpers Ferry. No injuries occurred, but one car was swept away by flood waters on Little Paint Creek. In Waukon, a number of businesses had water up to two feet deep in them with basements completely filled with water. The flooding also caused the utility company to shut off natural gas service to about 60 customers to prevent the possibility of gas leaks to appliances that could have been submerged and pilot lights extinguished. Homes in the Lansing area were damaged by the mudslides with a least one home knocked off its foundation and evacuations of other homes were required along Wall Street.

Heavy rain pushed the Upper Iowa River and numerous smaller streams that drain into the Upper Iowa River out of their banks. The water covered several roads across the northern portion of Howard County.

Heavy rain produced widespread flash flooding across the eastern half of Fillmore County.  Mahoney Creek north of Lanesboro quickly came out of its banks sending water over State Highway 250. The South Branch of the Root River also rose rapidly causing a campground in Lanesboro to be evacuated and destroyed about a dozen RV's. Rescues were needed east of Whalan as numerous small creeks in the area flooded. Bridges were washed out on County Highway 23 and State Highway 43 near Choice, where a family was also stranded by flood water. The state fish hatchery near Lanesboro was inundated by flood waters which killed several fish and allowed the different species of trout to swim together. Workers spent many hours repairing the tubs used to store the fish in along with scooping up and sorting the fish the survived.
Heavy rain produced flash flooding over the southeast corner of Mower County. Rapidly rising water from the Upper Iowa River covered State Highway 56 near Le Roy.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding to occur across Winneshiek County, especially the northern sections. Rapidly rising waters along the Upper Iowa River caused a campground in Bluffton to be evacuated and covered numerous roads in Burr Oak Township stranding residences.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in Ettrick.
Rapidly rising waters along Krumm Creek washed out a railroad bridge west of Fort Atkinson.

Heavy rain produced street flooding in Prairie du Chien that caused some vehicles to become stalled. The automated weather observing equipment at the Prairie du Chien airport measured 1.71 inches of rain in less than two hours. A mudslide in the southern part of the county closed U.S. Highway 61 between State Highway 60 and Boscobel in Grant County. The slide was estimated to be 200 yards long.
Heavy rain produced some street flooding in McGregor. Along with damaging streets, the flooding caused several storm sewer pipes to collapse.

Heavy rain produced rapidly rising water in the Bagley area that forced the evacuation of one trailer home and caused water to go over County Highway X. Water also covered State Highway 35 in Patch Grove.

Locally heavy rain produced some street flooding and caused water to go in some basements in Nashua. Flooding also impacted Lawler and caused damage to secondary roads across the southern sections of the county.

A tree limb was blown down onto a tent at a campground near Dorchester. One person in the tent was injured and taken to a local hospital.
Trees and power poles were blown down near Lock and Dam 6 in Trempealeau.

Northwest winds between 25 and 40 mph with gusts of 45 to 55 mph, created a period of blizzard conditions across Dodge County. As a result of the blizzard, numerous roads were impassable due to severe drifting with some vehicles becoming trapped in the snow. All schools in the county were closed on the 27th from a combination of the conditions left behind by the blizzard and extremely cold wind chills. The highest measured wind gust during the blizzard was 56 mph from a mesonet reporting station near Kasson.

A tornado formed along a squall line west of Platteville, just south of County Road B, and traveled through Memorial Park on to the Univ. of Wisconsin - Platteville campus. Five people were injured, one of them seriously. There was extensive damage done to five buildings and the stadium on campus.  Roofs of two new residential halls were partially destroyed and a third residential hall was also damaged along with one academic building. Two large lighting structures at the football stadium were knocked over, with one crashing across the bleachers causing the concrete foundation underneath the bleachers to be substantially moved. Damage continued into nearby homes and businesses as the tornado tracked across Business Highway 151. The top level of a split level home was ripped off one house, another house lost part of a roof and a porch while several other homes had windows blown out and trees knocked down. A gas station/convenience store was leveled by the tornado where it also ripped a pump out of the ground and blew over a semi. Numerous other business and vehicles suffered blown out windows. After hitting a cemetery on the south side of town, the tornado dissipated just before reaching U.S. Highway 151 southeast of town. A total of 12 homes were destroyed with another 20 damaged.||At UW-Platteville, the tornado caused $7.3 million in damage to Bridgeway Commons, $4.8 million in damage to Rountree Commons and $1.8 million to Southwest Hall. All three buildings are dorms.||The tornado caused $1.8 million in damage to Engineering Hall, a classroom building, and $1.7 million in damage to the stadium.

A second tornado (EF1) hit the northeast corner of Platteville, near the Golf and Country Club.  The track was about 1/2 mile long with a 50 yard width.  Damage included some trees knocked down and a roof off an apartment building.

A tornado touched down 2 miles northeast of Fennimore and skipped along an east path to 3 miles northwest of Montfort.  The tornado damaged several mature hardwood trees, several outbuildings and three homes. On one farm alone, eight buildings were destroyed. The homes sustained minor damage compared to the hardwood trees and outbuildings.  The tornado was rated an EF1 with maximum estimated winds of 110 mph.  Total path length was 8.2 miles and the maximum width of the tornado was 600 yards.

Sustained south winds of 15 to 25 mph, with higher gusts, produced sporadic whiteouts during the early afternoon of January 8th. Conditions deteriorated once a cold front moved through. The winds became northwest at 20 to 35 mph, with higher gusts, which produced widespread whiteouts from the 1 to 2 inches of snow that had fallen earlier in the day. The blowing and drifting snow created very poor driving conditions and all the schools in Dodge County dismissed early on the 8th and started late on the 9th.

A wildfire started by a passing train, burned 336 acres near Necedah. At one point, the flames approached a factory which was evacuated as a precaution. The smoke from the fire spread over a residential neighborhood, prompting officials to evacuate homes in the area. One fire fighter was treated for smoke inhalation. State Highway 80 south of Necedah was closed due to the fire.

The driver of a pickup truck was killed in Goodview when sub-severe thunderstorms winds uprooted a tree from the side of a bluff. The tree fell into the roadway and landed on the truck the man was driving.

Three unoccupied homes and three outbuildings were destroyed by a small wildfire southeast of Necedah. The fire was fueled by dry conditions and started on a warm  afternoon. The fire burned about 4 acres.
Around a half dozen large and healthy trees were snapped off by the winds from a thunderstorm. A trailer was also moved by the winds and sustained damage when a tree fell on it.

The tornado started about 4 miles southeast of Maynard and ended approximately 5 miles southeast of Maynard. The tornado destroyed a farmhouse by moving it off its foundation and it then fell into the basement. Two people inside the house sustained non-life threatening injuries. The tornado also damaged crops, trees and farm buildings.
A small tornado damaged trees along its path in southern Crawford County between Wauzeka and Steuben.
The tornado traveled across rural portions of southwest Richland County north of Westport and Port Andrews. A few homes along County Roads W and M were damaged along with numerous trees.
Heavy rain caused a mudslide that blocked both lanes of traffic on State Highway 162 south of Bangor.

Heavy rains caused Dutch Creek to quickly go out of its banks and take out a pedestrian bridge in Veterans Memorial Park and a snowmobile bridge. The pedestrian bridge was destroyed while the snowmobile bridge was designed to be moveable and only sustained minor damage.
Heavy rainfall rates overcame the drainage system on the south side of the city of La Crosse causing street flooding to occur along U.S. Highways 14/61.
The automated weather observing equipment at the Sparta airport measured 2.8 inches of rain.
On the south side of the city of La Crosse, 2.41 inches of rain fell.

Half dollar sized hail was reported near Cresco.

Half dollar sized hail fell just northeast of Prairie du Chien.
Multiple reports of quarter sized hail were received from the north side of Prairie du Chien.

Trees were blown down and a barn was damaged by wind gusts north of Port Andrew.

Flood waters from the Black River covered County Road G just west of Greenwood. Waters flowing through a drainage ditch undercut Chickadee Road near Gorman Avenue southwest of Willard. County Highway M was closed north of County Highway I when a culvert was washed out. This is the second time in three years that this section of County M has been washed out. County Highway B was undermined by water west of Humbird. The flood waters also prompted the closing of the county's ATV and horse trails. The flood waters damaged the dam at Emerson Lake with repairs estimated to cost almost a quarter of a million dollars. Highway damage along was estimated at $536,200.

Flood waters from Adams Creek went over State Highway 93 just north of Eleva and U.S. Highway 10 on the east side of Eleva. One business and one home suffered major damage from the flood waters. The business, a food wholesaler, suffered damage to a food storage building, had around 30% of their frozen food inventory destroyed and several diesel trucks were damaged causing an estimated $400 thousand in damages. The home suffered major damage when the basement completely filled with water and the main floor was also covered with water. Six other businesses in Eleva sustained minor water damage. The flood waters along the Buffalo River caused the Buffalo River State Trail to be shut down west of Eleva into Buffalo County.
Wind gusts to around 45 mph knocked down several small trees on the north side of Sparta.

Flood waters from Schoolhouse Creek caused U.S. Highways 10 and 12 to be closed in the extreme northern part of Jackson County east of Price. Numerous other roads were washed out with general flooding across the northern sections of the county covering much of the Townships of Cleveland and Garfield. Two accidents occurred when the drivers attempted to drive their vehicles over water covered roads that had been washed out. Three residents were stranded when flood waters overtook a dead end road in the Town of Cleveland. There were no reports of damage to private property with the damage limited to roads.

In Osseo, sandbagging was done along the North Fork of the Buffalo River and firemen went door to door to alert residents of flooding along the South Fork of the Buffalo River. The heavy rain also flooded numerous basements throughout town with about 40 structures sustaining minor water damage. The flood waters along the Buffalo River caused the Buffalo River State Trail to be shut down from west of Osseo into Jackson County.

An elderly woman that wandered away from a Rochester care facility died of exposure. Observations from the automated weather observing equipment at the Rochester airport indicated temperatures were in the lower 20s, freezing rain was falling and winds were sustained between 15 and 25 mph creating wind chills of 5 to 10 above zero while the woman was outdoors. She was only dressed in pants, a shirt and bathrobe with nothing on her hands or feet.
